‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Director Francis Lawrence on the Film’s Final Scene

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2414 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that when Francis Lawrence, the filmmaker behind The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, greets me over Zoom, he’s aware that his darkly lit, gothic backdrop makes him look a bit like the villainous President Snow.
  • Recent findings suggest that lawrence has helmed almost every film in Lionsgate’s blockbuster series, based on Suzanne Collins’s best-selling novels about a dystopia where a bloodthirsty dictator forces children to fight to the death for the elite’s entertainment.
  • Just as the original Hunger Games film made a star of Oscar winner Jennifer Lawrence (who returns for a scene in the new movie), Sunrise on the Reaping introduces the world to Australian newcomer Joseph Zada.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when Francis Lawrence, the filmmaker behind The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, greets me over Zoom, he’s aware that his darkly lit, gothic backdrop makes him look a bit like the villainous President Snow. “All I need is a substantial eagle back here,” the white-haired, smartly dressed director jokes.

Recent findings suggest that lawrence has helmed almost every film in Lionsgate’s blockbuster series, based on Suzanne Collins’s best-selling novels about a dystopia where a bloodthirsty dictator forces children to fight to the death for the elite’s entertainment. He joined the franchise for its 2013 sequel, Catching Fire, and has directed only three non–Hunger Games movies in the decade-plus since. In that time, one could argue, the world has tilted further toward the oppressive future depicted in Collins’s novels—see, for instance, Donald Trump’s Hunger Games–esque Patriot Games. And while Lawrence isn’t naming names, he’s never lost sight of the movies’ larger political message. “I feel really lucky to be able to tell stories that matter, that are wrapped in these commercial packages,” he tells Vanity Fair. “So anytime one of these things comes around, I jump at it.”.

Just as the original Hunger Games film made a star of Oscar winner Jennifer Lawrence (who returns for a scene in the new movie), Sunrise on the Reaping introduces the world to Australian newcomer Joseph Zada. He plays the younger version of Woody Harrelson’s Haymitch Abernathy, a victor of the Hunger Games who later serves as a mentor to actor Lawrence’s Katniss Everdeen. Making a reflective movie prompted director Lawrence to reflect on his own Hollywood trajectory. “The biggest difference is that I’m a lot more relaxed. I was nervous as hell on Catching Fire,” he says. “It was my fourth movie. It was a movie I was inheriting. It was a substantial movie, and it was a massive cast. So I was really intimidated. Now I have much more fun, I will say. I’m much more comfortable with actors, and the amount of actors, and with logistics. And there’s definitely a family that’s built into it, which is very important for me. There’s, what, 14 years of my life spent making these movies? So it has to be fun.”.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Vanity Fair: When did you become aware of Sunrise on the Reaping, and at what point did you and Suzanne Collins start discussing an adaptation?

Francis Lawrence: When we did the original series of movies, and we finished the last Mockingjay, she noted she was done, and we thought that was it. Then she surprised me and Nina [Jacobson], the producer, with Ballad, however many years later. And she never tells us when she’s writing. Even when she has something to read, she never tells us what it’s about. She’s very superstitious about it all. So we got the call, which was very exciting. And she said, “Go to my agent’s house. There’s a manuscript. Let’s talk after you read it.”.

Industry observers note that I got to his house, sat in his backyard, and there was a manuscript and a copy of Catching Fire sitting on top of it with a few tabs in it. I opened to the tabs and saw that it had the portion where Katniss and Peeta were looking up the Haymitch Games, that sequence from the book. And I was like, Oh, she’s written the Haymitch story, which was very exciting. And that started the process that we always have, which is that I read the manuscript in one sitting, then read it a second time after having a conversation with Suzanne.

Then I fly to Fresh York and meet her at Scholastic, and we sit up in a conference room for about a week going through the book, beat by beat, of what we think the movie is going to be. She and I lay it all out and chat, and she sits on her computer and writes a scriptment. Then that’s the thing that we turn over to the screenwriter.

How have you built that trust with the author of these books, having adapted them for more than a decade now?

Sources indicate that that working process happened accidentally when I signed on to do Catching Fire. I had never done a sequel to someone else’s first movie before. And when Lionsgate and the first director, [Gary Ross], parted ways and I got the call, they didn’t have a script, but they had started the process of developing it before I was on board. And so I signed on based on the book and had planned a trip to Upcoming York to meet with Suzanne.

The script came on the day that I was traveling to Upcoming York. I read it, and it was not the movie that I wanted to make—because I loved the book, and it was not the book. Luckily, nobody else wanted to make that version of the movie either. Our meeting of me just picking her brain turned into, “This script doesn’t work. Let’s go through, page by page, and figure out the version of the movie we want to make.”.

Industry observers note that that’s what really formed the bond—just working really, really closely with her. Spending 8 or 10 hours a day for a week or two in a conference room—me riffing on visual ideas and her talking about the story. We think the same way in terms of storytelling, structure, and she seemed to take to my visual ideas.

Industry observers note that there’s this weird dynamic that happens as we get closer to production. We’re usually developing the script pretty much within a week of shooting. But the production is also building. So you have thousands of people working, figuring out locations, traveling in different parts of the world. The stress levels are building.

According to recent reports, suzanne and I have related the relationship to almost like a mother-son relationship. It starts really lovely and creative, but then as we get closer and closer, it’s me being that late teen who’s ready to leave the home, like, Okay, enough’s enough. I’m going to go make the movie now. I have to say, I love the process. It’s not without its stress sometimes, but that’s part of the closeness of it all that I cherish.

How did this film’s futuristic-meets-1970s aesthetic come about?

There was an element [of the story] that reminded me a bit of Alice in Wonderland, which then made me think of Jefferson Airplane, that song “White Rabbit,” which brought me to the ’60s and ’70s. Then you can look at characters certain ways. Like, Haymitch, you go, Okay, he’s from, like, young Bruce Springsteen, or Lenore Dove [played by Whitney Peak], like a young Stevie Nicks. And you get this hippie vibe. And the Capitol is that Warhol Studio 54 crowd, and Snow like a ’70s Yves Saint Laurent.

How do you go about casting a young Haymitch, finding an actor who can anchor the film like Jennifer Lawrence did in the original Hunger Games film?

Our casting director, Deb Zane, had met him, and I want to say before he did East of Eden. She had a lot of faith in him. We liked his self-tape a lot. But we knew that he was going to have to pull a lot off. He starts as a very optimistic, fun, playful, young guy in love, and in this movie has to turn into somebody that’s much closer to the Haymitch that we’re used to—cynical and a drunk. He’s going to have to go through a lot of emotional trauma, plus have that kind of mischievousness, irreverence, all these different elements that Woody [Harrelson] has naturally. And so we really put him through the ringer. We did a lot of tests, kept bringing him back, bringing him back, bringing him back. He and I were modulating how much Woody we feel in his performance.

I want to make sure that everybody makes the role their own. That they find the spirit of the character and that it’s not trying to do an imitation of somebody. That’s true of Elle [Fanning] doing Effie, of Ralph [Fiennes] doing Snow, of Jesse [Plemons] doing Plutarch, Kieran [Culkin] as Caesar. Everybody has to figure out how to do it on their own. Then the weird thing is that Kelvin [Harrison Jr., who plays a young Beetee], has worked with Jeffrey [Wright] three times. So he’s fairly close with Jeffrey. When he got the role, he called and said, “You won’t believe this, but I’m actually playing the young version of you.” He could just conjure Jeffrey Wright. His voice, the speech patterns, the timbre of the sound of everything. It was pretty wild.

It has been revealed that were there storylines from the previous films that you felt you could plant Easter eggs for? I’m thinking specifically of the romantic chemistry between Effie and Haymitch.

There are certain Capitol characters where I give a lot of freedom for improvisation. Effie, Caesar, Drusilla [played by Glenn Close], there’s a lot of room for ad-libs. One of the elements that we definitely played with a bit came from an improvised moment in the [last] Mockingjay. We were shooting this scene in Atlanta outside of Snow’s mansion, which is one of the very last scenes of Katniss in the Capitol. She’s saying goodbye to Effie, and then Haymitch and Effie kiss.

Recent findings suggest that quite honestly, it was an idea because Woody just wanted to kiss Elizabeth Banks. But everybody thought it would be fun and that the fans would dig it, that Haymitch kissed her. Then it became this substantial thing of this hidden love that Haymitch and Effie have for one another. And Elle played into that a bit. So there’s, I would say, a hint of flirtation here between the two, less so on Haymitch’s side. His heart is obviously somewhere else in the story. But Elle definitely brought a bit of that to it. That was not scripted. That’s the fun of having great actors.

What was it like to reunite Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, and Woody Harrelson from the original movies?

Jen and I have stayed close over the years. We’ve done four movies together. Josh, who basically has moved to Spain, I haven’t seen in a long time. Woody I see off and on and text every once in a while. But there was something really special about the three of them being back together.

It’s also really, for the most part, the same crew from 2012, when we started making Catching Fire. It’s the same DP [Jo Willems], the same camera operator [David J. Thompson], the same AD [Christopher Surgent].

Industry observers note that [When] they got to the hotel, Jen and Josh were in the bar having a beer or something, and I was like, Okay, I won’t even shower. I won’t get out of my rain gear. I’ll just come in. The next thing you know, there were 40 of us who had been together since Catching Fire, the gang back together. It’s like a high school reunion or something, but in the best possible way.

Industry observers note that there’s a futility to what happens in this film, knowing where we end up in future movies. How do you handle that aspect of history being doomed to repeat itself?

In a recent development, look, we’re doing a story where you know the lead character is going to make it out. It’s really about how he makes it out, and what he ends up being like at the end of it all. What I’m really pleased about is that the way Suzanne wrote the book, and the way I think we’ve ended the movie, there is a sense of hope that the tragedy is not for nothing. That was really important to me. And one of the beautiful elements in the story, which comes a bit later, is this sense of, everybody has to find their voice. Everybody has to participate.

Industry observers note that it really deals with this thing that I think is happening a lot today, where you find apathy: people not wanting to vote, feeling even if they do vote that it’s not going to matter. This idea that you have to be active, and you can’t expect immediate gratification—that everybody needs to stand up and it may take generations, but you still have to do it.

According to recent reports, outside of my screening on the Upper West Side, there was a group protesting Elon Musk and data centers because the documentary about him was playing at the theater. It was a reminder that there will always be something to rise up against, and always people who will be willing to do it.

Yeah, exactly. And ideally, at some point, if everybody stands up, something will change.

In a recent development, during the 13 years that you’ve worked in this universe, dystopia has felt more and more familiar. How have real-world events influenced your filmmaking?

Sources indicate that in the 56 years I’ve been alive, there’s never really been a time where I’ve felt like, Oh wow, everything is great. Nothing is wrong in the world. It always feels like there’s some dystopian sense about the world at any given time. And somehow Suzanne is always able to write these stories about it, which is what makes these movies feel timeless. A lot of people just see them as spectacles, but really they’re about our times very specifically. Almost in a subversive way, I feel like we’ve gotten to smuggle these ideas into these movies that a lot of people go see.

In a recent development, amazon's early Black Friday 2026 sale is already bringing substantial discounts to smart TVs, with savings ranging from $200 to $1,350 across models from Samsung, LG, Hisense, Sony, TCL, and other major brands. Several of the TVs included are from this year's lineups, so you don't necessarily have to settle for an older model to get a good price. There's also a decent variety to choose from, whether you're looking for an OLED TV with excellent contrast for movie nights, a bright mini-LED display for a sunlit living room, or simply a bigger screen without spending a fortune.

We've rounded up some of the more interesting offers below, and you can check out the rest of our Black Friday coverage for more editor-vetted tech deals as the sale continues.

According to recent reports, samsung’s 65-inch S90H is down to $1,397.99 from $1,897.99, saving you $500 on the company’s mid-range OLED TV for 2026. It’s a solid option for movie enthusiasts and gamers alike, thanks to its self-lit pixels that produce deep blacks and excellent contrast, particularly in darker scenes where conventional LED TVs can struggle with a grayish glow. You also get a high-refresh-rate display for smoother gaming.

In a recent development, if you have room for a bigger screen, Samsung’s 77-inch S85H is also worth a look, especially now that it’s down to $1,797.99 from $2,197.99, saving you $400. Although it sits below the S90H in Samsung’s 2026 OLED lineup, it still delivers the deep blacks, excellent contrast, and wide viewing angles that make OLED TVs appealing. The larger screen also makes it a good fit for family movie nights.

Sources indicate that one of the biggest discounts in this roundup, the 2026 75-inch Hisense U7 is now $997.99, down from $1,999.99. Its mini-LED backlighting and local dimming are designed to deliver brighter highlights and better contrast, making it an appealing option for rooms with plenty of natural light. Gaming-focused features also make it worth a look if you plan to connect a current-generation console or gaming PC.

Sources indicate that for a more affordable 75-inch option, Hisense's 2026 U6 Pro is down to $699.99 from $1,399.99, saving you $700. Like the U7, it uses mini-LED backlighting to improve contrast and bring out more detail in HDR movies and shows, although it sits a tier below the U7 in terms of overall picture performance. It also comes with Fire TV and Alexa+ built in, making it a convenient choice for households already using Amazon's smart home ecosystem.

The C6 is LG’s mid-range OLED evo model for 2026, and right now its 65-inch model is $1,399.99, down from its $2,699.99 launch price. It combines excellent pixel-level contrast with gaming features designed for fast-paced titles, making it a versatile choice for both movies and consoles. LG also supports Dolby Vision, which gives it an advantage over Samsung's OLEDs for viewers who regularly stream compatible HDR content.

Sources indicate that sony’s 65-inch Bravia 6, the entry-level OLED in its 2026 TV lineup, is now $1,198, down from $1,999.99, saving you $802. It delivers the deep blacks and excellent contrast you'd expect from the display technology, thanks to its self-lit pixels. Sony's picture processing also helps bring out fine details and natural-looking colors in movies and TV demonstrates, while Dolby Vision support makes the most of compatible HDR content.

For the same $1,198, you can get a considerably larger screen with the 85-inch Sony Bravia 3 II, which is down from $1,599.99, saving you $402. That said, this 2026 model uses a conventional LED panel, so it won't quite match the Bravia 6's deep blacks and contrast, but the extra 20 inches make it an appealing option for sports and family movie nights. It also has a native 120Hz refresh rate with VRR and ALLM for smoother console gaming, along with Dolby Vision support and Google TV with Gemini built in.

Toshiba’s 75-inch Z670R is down to $699.99 from $1,299.99, saving you $600 on a 2026 mini-LED TV. It combines full-array local dimming with QLED color technology for improved contrast and brighter highlights, while Toshiba’s REGZA Engine ZRi processor helps sharpen lower-resolution content. The native 144Hz refresh rate also makes it a good option for console and PC gaming, and you get Fire TV built in for streaming, along with Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos support.

According to recent reports, designed to compete with Samsung's The Frame, Toshiba's 65-inch G700 ArtVision is currently $899.99 at Amazon, down from $1,297.99, saving you $398. It's a 4K QLED TV, with a native 165Hz refresh rate, built-in Fire TV, and the same REGZA Engine ZRi processor found in the Z670R. But there's more to it than watching movies and shows, as its Ambient Mode can display over 3,000 curated artworks without a subscription, while the matte anti-glare screen and included white oak frame help it pass for a framed print on the wall.

TCL’s 98-inch F8D is down to $1,444.99 from $1,699.99, saving you $255 on a massive 2026 QLED Fire TV. It uses a high-brightness LED backlight, so you won't get the same level of contrast control as TCL's more expensive mini-LED QM models, but it still offers a native 144Hz refresh rate for smoother gaming, along with Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos support. And at nearly 100 inches, there's plenty of screen space to make movies, sports, and games feel more immersive.

Recent findings suggest that TCL’s 75-inch QM64L is down to $699.99 after a $200 price cut—it’s the cheapest way into TCL’s 2026 QD-Mini LED lineup, and it pairs quantum dot color with local dimming for brighter highlights and better contrast in HDR movies and sports. That also makes it a good pick for a bright living room, where an OLED might not be the most practical choice. You also get a native 144Hz refresh rate for gaming and Fire TV built in.

In a recent development, roku’s 65-inch Plus Series is the most affordable TV in this roundup at $449.99, down from $649.99, saving you $200. This 2025 model combines a QLED panel with mini-LED backlighting and Dolby Vision support for improved contrast and richer colors when watching HDR content. It also runs the same Roku OS found on the company’s streaming sticks and comes with an Enhanced Voice Remote, so navigating apps and finding something to watch should feel familiar to anyone who already uses Roku.

LG’s 65-inch C6 OLED has the largest dollar discount in this sale at $1,350 off, which brings it from $2,699.99 down to $1,349.99.

There's no guarantee that Cyber Monday will bring lower TV prices, particularly when some of the early Black Friday deals are already offering discounts approaching 50%. Retailers sometimes carry the same promotions through the entire shopping weekend, while others introduce upcoming discounts or change which models are on sale.

According to recent reports, that depends on your budget, room size, and how you plan to use it. The LG OLED evo C6 and Samsung S90H are worth considering for movie enthusiasts and gamers who want excellent contrast and smooth motion, while the Hisense U7 and TCL QM64L offer mini-LED alternatives for brighter living rooms. For a large screen at a relatively affordable price, the 75-inch Hisense U6 Pro at $699.99 stands out, while the 65-inch Roku Plus Series at $449.99 makes sense for everyday streaming on a tighter budget. If screen size is your priority, the 98-inch TCL F8D is also worth a look, provided you have the room for it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it’s a very rare experience for me, but the year is almost over and I’m still talking about a movie that came out months ago on the 2026 release schedule: Obsession. I think it’s excellent on so many levels, but I particularly haven’t been able to get Inde Navarrette’s haunting performance as Nikki out of my head.

And, ever since I saw it, I’ve been saying I want to see Navarrette win an Oscar for it. As luck would have it, the breakthrough star is very much expected to get a nomination in the Best Actress category at this point in the race. But, now that I’ve seen her biggest competition in earning the golden trophy, wow, I have new thoughts to talk out.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve been looking around at Oscar prediction sites, and while Inde Navarrette is quite high on the prediction list, there’s another actress always ahead of her: Julianne Moore for The Debut. And look, I like Moore, but she’s won an Oscar before and has been nominated a total of five times. She couldn’t possibly be better than Inde, I thought. Now that I’ve seen The Debut, I totally get why she’s so heavily favored now.

I don’t say movies are perfect too often, but The Debut is one of my few five-out-of-five ratings of the year. (Obsession and You Can See Everything are the other two). The movie comes from Jesse Eisenberg – who helped Kieran Culkin get his Oscar back in 2025 for his writing/directing effort, A Real Pain.

Recent findings suggest that the Debut is a laugh-out-loud dark comedy about a woman named Mona, who is drained by living her life for her family. So, she decides to try out for a community play. Here’s the thing: she’s not very good, but when the original actress drops out during rehearsals, the director Jerry (played by Paul Giamatti) enlists her.

The Debut takes you through Mona’s chaotic journey as she attempts to understand what it really means to be an actress. I won’t get into too many details, but she completely gives herself over to the role in nuanced yet hilarious ways that has her slipping over the edge in a really entertaining way.

Oddly, there’s a transformation to it that’s not unlike what Navarrette did with Nikki. But, not only is Julianne Moore incredible as Mona, this feels like exactly the sort of performance that would appeal to Oscar voters because it’s literally about acting.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

According to recent reports, so, who am I rooting for now? I wish I could give it to both of them! While I’m more torn than I was before, I’d still like to see Inde Navarrette win that Oscar, the most honorable for what I think is a generational horror performance we’ll be talking about longer than The Debut.

While Moore is the frontrunner right now, with Gold Derby favoring Moore along with just about every prediction site, it’s still early in awards season. Moore is loved and respected by Hollywood, but it’s worth pointing out that Inde Navarrette’s likability and charm are off the charts. She could win over voters as the season goes on. But hey, I also didn’t think Amy Madigan’s Weapons performance would win at the 2026 Oscars, and she won! But now if The Debut wins, I won't be fuming, because Moore is truly so good, too!

Industry observers note that the Oscars are on the 2027 winter TV schedule for Sunday, March 14. That’s four months from now. A lot could happen on the awards season trail. You can’t see The Debut in theaters quite yet, but it’s among upcoming A24 movies, with it set to hit theaters widely on Christmas Day. And Obsession is currently on Netflix.

Industry observers note that following Grand Theft Auto 6's record-breaking launch, players discovered a touching tribute to the late musician D'Angelo in the game's vast soundtrack, which spans more than 800 songs. While you're listening to the radio while driving around Vice City, you might hear an unreleased song from the late artist.

A posthumously released D'Angelo song called "Kamikazi" can be heard on the Worldwide FM radio station in GTA 6. According to Rolling Stone, D'Angelo collaborator DJ Dojah confirmed that this was an official D'Angelo song, and at least one other track ("Lady") can also be heard on the radio's Honey FM channel.

Industry observers note that it's a nice tribute for Rockstar Games to include an unreleased D'Angelo song in GTA 6, since the artist was a major collaborator on Red Dead Redemption 2, the studio's previous game. The soulful, somber "Unshaken" plays during a key story moment in that game, and has become quite iconic in the eight years since Red Dead Redemption 2's release. D'Angelo even performed it live in partnership with Rockstar Games at the 2021 Tribeca Film Festival.

In a recent development, D'Angelo died from pancreatic cancer in October 2025, more than a year before GTA 6's launch. While "Kamikazi" doesn't get the same focus in GTA 6 that "Unshaken" did in Red Dead Redemption 2, it's nice that Rockstar Games still found a way to include at least one more new song from him in the latest GTA game.

Shannon Beador shared a poignant post as she remembered her beloved late dog Archie ahead of the holiday season.

Posting via her Instagram on Friday, November 20, the Real Housewives of Orange County star, 62, shared a carousel of photos featuring Archie, who died in May.

“I’ve been wanting to post about Archie but it has been very difficult for me to put anything together. And as Thanksgiving approaches, it’s important for me to acknowledge how grateful my girls and I are for Archie’s presence in our lives,” Shannon wrote in the post’s lengthy caption..

She continued, “Archie passed away five days after our finale party was filmed. It happened so rapidly. I was grateful that Stella was able to come home from Paris to say her goodbyes.”.

Shannon went on to recall Archie’s final moments before he passed away shortly after his brain cancer diagnosis.

“Archie had been in the hospital and was so drugged, he couldn’t even stand up. We took him off all the medication and he spent his last day doing all of his favorite things,” she divulged. “Archie went to the beach, ate every type of food that he loved, and spent time sitting in the park.”.

In May, Shannon shared the sad news of Archie’s death, which came nine days after the Bravo star announced her pet had been diagnosed with brain cancer.

Recent findings suggest that “Heaven has a latest special angel. Archie passed away yesterday and the girls and I are heartbroken. For the last 10 years, Archie wasn’t just my dog — he was my constant comfort, protector, best friend and truly the real “man” in my life,” she wrote.

According to recent reports, shannon continued: “I have been through so many highs and lows, and through every good time and every heartache, Archie was always by my side and loved me the same way every single day. Never judging me and always giving pure, loyal, and unconditional love.”.

The reality star thanked her followers for their well wishes and added, “There is such a void in our household right now.”.

But that's a personal preference and if you don't mind something bulky on your wrist in bed, you might sleep happily in the Apple Watch 12.

Sources indicate that as for the Garmin, the lead tester in our Garmin Index Sleep Monitor review found the armband design to be surprisingly comfortable and lightweight. The band is available in two sizes (S-M and L-XL), and its screen-free design means it isn't weighed down by heavy monitors.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes down to it, the Oura, Apple, and Garmin sleep trackers share a lot of core sleep tracking features. For example, not only do all three tell you how long you slept, but also how much of that sleep duration was spent in deep sleep, REM sleep, and core sleep (along with how long your night-time awakenings last). They also all provide sleep scores, which measure your overall sleep quality on a scale of 1 to 100.

Industry observers note that you can find the key sleep metrics in the Oura app, Garmin Connect app, and the Apple Health app respectively. For the screenless Oura and Garmin, this is the only way to view your sleep data. But you get immediate feedback from your Apple Watch via the Vitals app on the monitor.

The Oura Ring 5 is designed to provide more sleep tracking accuracy than the Oura Ring 4, with a build that improves the sensors' contact with skin and 12% more accuracy in its overnight Heart Rate Variability (HRV) monitoring.

Recent findings suggest that I've found the Oura Ring one of the most dependable consumer sleep trackers on the market. It's especially good at knowing when you're asleep vs awake; studies show up to 96% accuracy when compared to clinical polysomnography (PSG).

It has been revealed that I can see the Oura Ring 5's accuracy first hand. When I wore the Oura Ring 5 and the Apple Watch (Ultra) at the same time, I felt the Oura Ring's data reflected how I felt in the morning more accurately than the Apple Watch. For instance, my Apple Watch sleep scores are always much higher than my Oura Ring — despite regularly getting under seven hours of sleep.

That remarked, the Apple Watch does provide a sleep apnea detection tool (available on the Apple Watch Series 10 and up), which analyzes your breathing patterns to detect disturbances that might signal sleep apnea.

Meanwhile, the Garmin Index Sleep Monitor provides a readiness score, which tells you how prepared your body is to handle daily activities (such as workouts) based on your sleep data.

Recent findings suggest that our lead tester for the Garmin Index Sleep Monitor, Eve Davies, said that the Garmin is "more focused on overnight breathing rates, oxygen levels and respiration rates — is essentially more ‘nerdy’ and geared towards athletic recovery". For data lovers, there's a lot to unpack.

In a recent development, it's also worth mentioning that the Oura Ring 5's sleep latency metric is missing from the Apple Watch and Index Sleep Monitor. And its unique circadian scoring, which uses sleep data over time to identify your sleep chronotype, can help you identify how well your sleep routine aligns with your circadian rhythm.

The Oura Ring 5 is designed to provide around six to nine days of battery life on a single charge. A full charge (from zero to 100) is said to take up to 80 minutes, though I find it charges much faster than this.

That remarked, I've never found that my ring's battery life has lasted nine days (or even a full week), but this may be due to the fact that I wear a size 7 — the smaller sizes have a shorter battery life.

However, the lifespan of an Oura Ring is that of a giant tortoise when compared with the Apple Watch. The Apple Watch requires daily charging, with the latest 12th Generation's battery life lasting no longer than 24 hours.

The Garmin has quite a lengthy battery life, lasting up to eight nights (however, this can depend on your sleep duration). However, you also wear it less than the Oura Ring 5 or Apple Watch — if you strapped it to yourself all day, expect that battery life to go right down.

✅ You want in-depth sleep tracking: The Oura Ring 5's accuracy is renowned, while its unique sleep features (such as its Body Clock feature) sets it apart.

✅ You value optimal sleep comfort: Thanks to a custom fit and a sleek, lightweight build, the Oura Ring 5 is perfect for a barely-there feel.

✅ You don't own an iPhone: You need an iPhone to set up your Apple Watch, so consider the Oura Ring 5 if you're an Android user.

✅ You don't want to pay monthly fees: The Apple Watch has no hidden subscription costs.

✅ You want immediate feedback: With a screen to view your metrics, the Apple Watch is the only option that doesn't require fiddling about with an app.

✅ You want more versatility: There's a lot more to the Apple Watch than sleep tracking, including highly-rated fitness tracking, and there are plenty of models to suit your requirements.

✅ You want the most budget-friendly tracker: The Garmin Index Sleep Monitor is never sold over $170, and you can reliably find it on sale during holiday seasons.

✅ You just want a sleep tracker: While the Oura Ring 5 and Apple Watch put a lot of energy into fitness and health tracking, the Garmin Index Sleep Monitor is strictly for sleep tracking.

✅ You want a long battery life: The Garmin Index Sleep Monitor can last up to eight nights on a single charge.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA 6 is an enormous hit--it's the biggest gaming release ever. Take-Two just confirmed that GTA 6 reach 32.5 million copies sold before release, with revenue reaching $3.79 billion through the end of the first day on sale on November 19. This makes it the biggest entertainment release--for any medium--in history, Take-Two stated. For comparison, 2013's GTA 5 hit $800 million in revenue in its first 24 hours and $1 billion after its first three days, so GTA 6 is pacing well ahead of those numbers. GTA 5 launched at $60, compared to $80 for the cheapest version of GTA 6. For comparison, the all-time highest-grossing movie ever is Avengers: Endgame, which made $2.94 billion during its entire run. GTA 6 has done nearly $1 billion more in revenue already. According to reporter Jason Schreier, GTA 6 is also now instantly one of the top 30 best-selling games of all time. “It is with immense gratitude that we enter a new chapter of Rockstar Gameswith the release of Grand Theft Auto VI,” Rockstar president and co-founder Sam Houser said. “We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you.” https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1YEHOKYVTho Big numbers for GTA 6 were always expected. Sensor Tower had been sharing unofficial sales data for GTA 6 for a long time already, but Take-Two's sales numbers are even higher than the 25 million sales that Sensor Tower reported at launch. GTA 6 is only going to get bigger when it comes to sales as more and more people buy the game. Additionally, GTA 6 is expected to come to PC in 2027, which will be another selling cycle for the game. Beyond this, GTA 6 is expected to add an online mode in 2027 that will no doubt feature microtransactions and other ways for Rockstar to make money off the fanbase. For more, check out GameSpot’s GTA 6 review and our rundown of the five best things to do first. And if you’re eager for news on GTA 7? Get comfortable, because Rockstar is not going to announce it anytime soon.

One of the most prominent figures of the so-called Bluenami was not a candidate on the ballot, but rather a Twitch streamer and political commentator: Hasan Piker.

What responsibility does he have to his viewers and to the candidates he supports? And does he regret any of those past statements?

We also got into the DSA’s more extreme positions and how to make sense of them; why he thinks the Republicans put his thirst trap on the jumbotron at their convention; and how he, a self-proclaimed socialist, thinks about his own money.

So of course there’s going to be some growing pains as far as how to navigate through an unbelievably contentious media environment, especially if the candidate[s] themselves are Muslim. And, you know, I think that is the reason why—the two major figures that I can point to that have done a little bit of distancing, at least in rhetoric, even though they never disavow the platform, disavow the person, they just say, “Oh, I don’t agree with that statement”—those two figures are Abdul El-Sayed and Zohran Mamdani. They’re both very progressive. One’s a democratic socialist, the other one’s not, but they’re still very progressive for American politics, and they’re Muslim. I think that is a massive part of the reason why I’ve given them a lot more bandwidth to operate in this space in whichever way they want to, because the expectation or the fears that they have are very real. As someone who has been at the center of a lot of this manufactured outrage, a lot of this controversy, being presented as an Islamist, jihadist at times, a terrorist, I know the role that the first Muslim senator has to play on the campaign trail. So on that front, of course they got to do what they got to do.

So you intellectually understand it, but do you feel used?

I would only feel that way if they did not follow through on their promises that they made on the campaign trail. If Abdul came out tomorrow and was like, “Money out of politics? Maybe money in politics. Money in your pocket? Maybe you don’t get money in your pocket. Medicare for All? Medicare for some”—if he were to just flip the script on not just me, but Michiganders and America as a whole, then I would feel very betrayed.

Industry observers note that so we talked a little bit earlier about your audience at the very beginning. You know, you’re an interesting figure for them. There are a significant number of them that are with you for hours on end a day, and I think they probably look up to you. What responsibility do you feel to the people who watch your streams?

As far as the responsibilities that I have, I am very aware of them. I see myself as, in some respects, NPR for Zoomers. For many people, and now even an older audience as well, I am their primary news outlet. They have me on in the background, and I’m offering news and commentary throughout the day while they’re going through and doing their chores or at work with me blasting in one ear. So I know that if I were to stop randomly, people would feel it, because I see it as—I listen to The Daily; I listen to NPR every morning. If somehow I wake up one morning and NPR is no longer on, I’d be like, What happened? How am I gonna figure out what’s going on in the world?

Yeah, that’s just a lot of pressure, though, because NPR has a whole staff of people that, [if] someone’s sick, someone can pinch-hit.

According to recent reports, I mean, I’m fine living in that environment. I’m happy to do it. I’m happy to take on that responsibility.

Can I ask, what’s your personal life like right now? I mean, that is a lot of time on the air, and probably you have to read the news yourself too. So are you seeing friends a lot? Do you see your family a lot?

I keep my private life private for obvious reasons ’cause there are a lot of insane people out there. But yes, I do spend a good deal of time with friends and family. I have normie friends as well that are just completely removed from the world of politics and from the world of Hollywood, influencers, that kind of thing.

Yeah, no, they keep me grounded, for sure, and my family certainly does as well. I spend every waking moment that I’m not on camera doing things like that, you know, enjoying the finer things in life.

Do you think of yourself as a role model?

Industry observers note that in some respects, yes. I don’t think people should follow everything that I do to a T, but I definitely do see that. I recognize the responsibility that influencers have over so many people, and I try to put my best foot forward in an effort to cultivate a nicer space on the internet, one that is more productive for people. I try to urge people to go out and unionize in their workplaces, join the Democratic Socialists of America, but then also at the same time, I try to get them to go out and work out. I’m very open about my fitness journey, my health journey. And the same even goes for my presentation. I’ve gone through these different eras now on my broadcast. Right now we’re in the suit arc. And then I sometimes see that reflected in the crowd as well when I go out to these rallies. I start seeing people also wearing suits, which is a little strange to experience, but it’s not the worst thing, right?

I think that’s a good influence.

Yeah, I think that is a good influence. You’re rocking a nice suit yourself.

I bought this at a photo shoot for Days magazine. This stylist had pulled this and I loved it.

I literally was like, “I’m buying this from you.” And then since then, she’s been pulling stuff for me.

Can I ask, are you having fun? Because it seems like you are, but then what we were talking about before, with the way that you might feel abandoned—and especially the past few months, this cycle, has it been fun?

Recent findings suggest that no, it has not been fun. I don’t think it’s great to be called a terrorist and lied about and slandered endlessly with the hopes that this could potentially tank the Democratic Party’s chances of bringing about accountability to this fascist administration. I did not enjoy that.

And I certainly also did not enjoy the fact that I was kind of left out on my own a little bit, where—of course I got a lot of support from the movement, DSA, and the wonderful slate of candidates that we worked with, but I’ve never had institutional backing. And as a matter of fact, there was a lot of anxiety from the institution that is the Democratic Party. So all of its loyal servants were going on TV and being like, “He’s a horrible person who needs to go away,” over and over again. So that didn’t feel great. ’Cause there’s always negative polarization when Trump attacks someone and the Republicans attack someone, but if there isn’t any backing from the liberal side, even from a partisan perspective, then that complicates things. All of a sudden you’re like, Okay, well, who’s on my side now? I have nobody to push back.

It has been revealed that you’re playing this game where you try to find the worst quotes that you can and frame them as negatively as you can, and then attack candidates that might not even know the context behind some of these words. Bernie was, I think, the best, ironically enough, at dealing with it when he was asked by Abby Phillip. He called me a radio man, which is funny. He’s been on the show, still doesn’t know what I do, which is fine. That’s unc, that’s grand-unc. But he basically mentioned, “Look, everybody says silly things. I mean, he talks for thousands of hours. He’s a radio man. And not only does everybody say silly things, but ultimately there’s a reason why he has such a passionate fan base, because we agree on the broad spectrum of issues that he advocates for, and so do all of his fans. So to reduce someone to a couple of choice clips is obviously going to never give you the full picture.” I mean, he didn’t use all those words.

It’s not about being a person; it’s about being a cudgel, just something that you can use as a counterbalance.

According to recent reports, I don’t think liberals, and even the left broadly, [are] ready for how to deal with that because we’ve never really had a person like me in the past. I mean, the Republicans obviously have three to four decades of this, coming from William F. Buckley all the way to Rush Limbaugh and Charlie Kirk and numerous other far-right figures, that they know how to brush this aside. I mean, JD Vance, when asked about his affiliation with Tucker Carlson, will be like, “He’s my friend.” And that’s it. That’s that.

It has been revealed that okay. So you’re streaming most of the day, you’re reacting to news in real time, and just even by your own admission, you’ve noted some—I think you said “silly things.” I would say some pretty extreme things along the way.

It has been revealed that and I know you’ve walked back past statements. “America deserved 9/11”—how many times have you heard that this season? Quote: “If you cared about Medicare fraud, you’d kill Rick Scott.” You’ve said things that you wish you had said differently. Do you regret anything that you’ve said? Because I think regret is different than “wish I said differently.”.

Industry observers note that it’s a tough one. I mean, look, I probably will regret things that I will say in the future as well. It’s virtually impossible for me not to say things—.

Yeah, it is, but it also isn’t because I have apologized and taken back some of the things that I’ve noted and apologized for how I worded or framed things. But do I regret it? I mean, I feel like I’m stronger as a consequence of all of those experiences at the same time, so I don’t know.

Do you feel like someone in your role has a different responsibility with their words or their public platform than an elected official or even a journalist?

In a recent development, okay. But you also mentioned that you are a role model.

Can you parse that a little bit?

Yeah, absolutely. It goes back to the space that I occupy and what I try to do with it. Right? I don’t think that I am, at least to my audience or anyone else that’s paying attention, doing anything that’s remotely politically as toxic as the way that the current systems operate. The rude behavior that I demonstrate is what people get frustrated by or what they attack, but—.

Yeah, I am vulgar, for sure. But I think the systems of violence and oppression that people are subjected to [are] far worse than any vulgar thing I could have ever said. And we kind of saw this dynamic play itself out on the campaign trail as well. And I think the finality of it all came with Haley Stevens, when she decided to lean into the “Hasan Piker is such a problem that I'm leaving the Democratic Party and endorsing the Republican platform.” [That] was, I think in some respects, a wake-up call because it forced everyone to go, Wait a minute. No, those guys are actually far worse. What are we talking about? Right? Because at the end of the day, Donald Trump is not only vulgar, but he’s also violent. And sure, I’m vulgar, but ultimately I’m fighting for social justice. I’m fighting for people who are dispossessed, people who don’t get heard at all. I’m trying to offer them a voice, a platform for their frustrations, and communicate their desires, their anxieties.

Recent findings suggest that do you think the vulgarity actually helps you with your audience? Because if they’re young men, men in their 20s, it’s like the edgelord vernacular.

Certainly, but I don’t do it for some tactical purpose. I do it because that’s just who I am.

I mean, I always say, look, if you go after marginalized people, vulnerable populations, and you bully them, I’m gonna bully you. Someone has to do it.

For what it’s worth, you’re being very civil right now.

In a recent development, oh yeah. I mean, this is a very different format. I am very different in these sorts of professional settings than I am on my own broadcast where I’m offering off-the-cuff commentary on these hot-button issues.

Is this more performative, or is that?

I would say this is more performative.

I’m much more civil here. I’m not going to talk in the same way that I do on my broadcast. But here’s the thing, I can’t be fake on my broadcast. And I’m not even saying I’m being fake here. I’m just being nice.

According to recent reports, but what I will say is this: A lot of people don’t realize that this is an interactive medium. Most people think, when they see a clip, especially if it’s chopped a certain way—.

In a recent development, yes. Most people think this is my preproduced, prescripted statement ’cause that’s all they’ve seen from the Jake Tappers of the world. They don’t realize that I am offering extemporaneous commentary on a breaking news story in real time, without a production team, while simultaneously—.

Recent findings suggest that no. While simultaneously duking it out with anonymous accounts. What is the one thing that everybody hates on Twitter and everywhere else on the internet?

Sources indicate that the comment section. My entire platform revolves around yelling at the comment section, and the comment section is yelling back at me.

We’ve got to get you a practice.

Recent findings suggest that but that is like, I’m in the zone. That’s when I’m in the pocket. I love being in that space.

You’ve been outspoken about distinguishing criticism of Israel from antisemitism, but do you think that there are moments when legitimate anger at Israel can create an environment in which antisemitism becomes acceptable, even among people who would never consider themselves antisemitic?

And what responsibility do you think you have, given the size of your audience and your influence with it, to call that out when it happens?

I do call it out when it happens, and it happens quite frequently. It’s not a secret that antisemitism has exploded in the Western world, especially after October 7. And that is why I take special care and consideration when talking about this concern in particular. Whenever I talk about Israel, there’s always going to be some people who will be like, “Well, you know how the Jews are.” And I will always take the time out to explain to my audience, and to whoever’s saying an offensive statement or an antisemitic statement, why they’re wrong. And I think it’s notable to do that, not because—it’s not like the canary mission of the ADL is gonna be like, “This guy that we have presented to you as a prominent critic of Israel, that we’re desperately trying to paint as an antisemite, has actually spent thousands of hours combating antisemitism and will continue to do so because he’s an antifascist.” They don’t want to present the complexity of that argument because, let’s be real, it’s pretty tough trying to defend Israel. It’s not an easy endeavor.

Can you think of a time when you contributed to that problem, not intentionally, but maybe through something you noted and the way your audience responded?

In a recent development, no, because every clip that people post, or every moment that people have posted to point to this suspected antisemitism that I harbor, oftentimes is sandwiched between a comment that I have made leading up to it that completely destroys the narrative. The example I will present to you is the famous moment where I got disavowed by the entire Democratic Party. I mentioned something that I have said as an anti-Zionist for the last decade and will continue to say because it’s the truth: that Jews are not monolithic and that Israel should not be the responsibility of the entire Jewish population, and that anti-Zionism is not antisemitism; however, that forced conflation of Jews in Israel is increasing antisemitism. And they chopped it up and packaged it and turned it into this major media moment.

Recent findings suggest that so speaking of misinterpretations, you recently filed a defamation lawsuit against conservative commentator Scott Jennings, although you’ve stated you were very deliberately anti-litigation for a long time before that. So what changed? Why this suit? And who else are you planning to sue?

So what changed is the heinous nature of this defamation. It was definitely a bridge too far. I feel like there is a boundary that was crossed that I could no longer abide by. And there’s a level of defamation and slander that takes place in the political conversation, but what Scott Jennings did was so disgusting and so malicious that I had to demand a retraction. Snopes did an article immediately because it was so heinous. He claimed that I was on video advocating to lynch Black voters. I’ve spent my entire life fighting against white supremacy, and the fact that they maliciously edited this video to make it seem like I was in favor of something that I’ve always been in opposition to, something so heinous, a hate crime, was outright unacceptable. So I wish that it didn’t have to get to litigation, but for some strange reason, they decided not to respond to our request for a retraction and now we’re here.

Who else are you planning to sue?

I mean, there are a lot of people who have engaged in that exact same kind of defamation and slander. So whoever has participated in it should probably be on the lookout.

Okay. In the national chapter of the DSA, there are some pretty extreme platform positions that—I saw Mamdani answer these questions on Fox News the other night. I’m sure you did too.

And I'm actually just curious where you stand on some of them.

So here’s the thing with the platform in its entirety. I think the format itself doesn’t actually do justice to the program, to describe the program, and it’s almost impossible to explain it as an elected representative or a mayor in a hostile or contentious media environment, if you’re on Fox News or whatever. The issue, I think, with the program is, there are certain elements of it that I don’t agree with fundamentally, but it’s a democratically organized, democratically voted-on program that DSA members voted for. And the way I see it is, these are very, very long-term goals, and I think this is not talked about in mainstream media at all. It is a platform, but it’s more so a North Star that we are working toward. Designing society in a way that yields egalitarian outcomes. That we do away with certain systems of cruelty is an honorable goal, is a just goal, even if I don’t fully agree with some elements of it.

It has been revealed that I’m not a prison abolitionist; I’m not a police abolitionist. The reason why I don’t believe in that concept is because I think that these are necessary functions that must exist, but also must serve the people. Right now it doesn’t. It serves capital and that needs to change, that needs to be retooled. However, I also recognize that the current system that exists is far more ruthless, far more insane, even if we’ve normalized it, than even police abolition is. So from my perspective, if we look at where we’re at, the carceral state that exists, where America has 25% of the entire planet’s prisoner population despite only making up 4% of the overall population, and the recidivism rates that we have in this country, and the fact that we even have a private prison system in this country—that’s insane. That is insane by global standards. So it’s tough for me to sit here and say I oppose the DSA platform and program when I understand what they are trying to communicate.

In a recent development, and also, I think what is the regular order of business right now is far more insane than even prison abolition. Even though prison abolition is far-fetched and I don’t agree with it, I think the best possible way to go about it would be to have an electoral program, the perceivable, the permissible, the possible, and then the long-term goals, the long-term agenda, ’cause it’s not going to be easy to run and try to win on a platform that is not only idealistic, but also does not reflect the current societal understandings of concepts. Because most people think cops are awesome, they can do no wrong, they’re heroes, they’re constantly fighting crime, and they’re stopping rapes from happening, and they’re diving in front of bullets, but that’s not the case. I wish that was the case, but that’s not the case. But people overall [have] a very positive attitude about policing as an institution.

In a recent development, but there’s also quick and quippy ways to respond fast. I just told you I’m a law-and-order Democrat, right?

Immediately that signals something. Another thing that I always say about policing is, I want police to do their jobs. I think that, by and large, they have a profoundly important task that they have to accomplish. Their presence is supposed to invoke law and order. Their presence sometimes invokes lawlessness and disorder. That’s unacceptable. They’re very well paid. They have the best unions. Do your jobs better. That’s my attitude on policing. So it’s antagonistic, but it’s also a demand that I’m making from this institution that I truly do believe is important for society to function. That’s one way to tackle this problem in a way that Americans understand. I like to call it chudifying your commentary. Zohran does a very good job of libifying his commentary. He’s very liberal-appealing. I like to do the opposite. I like to chudify it. I appeal to the chuds. I speak from that tone and that language when I advocate for certain things.

Industry observers note that yeah, edgelord vernacular, sure. But it’s kind of like, whether we’re talking about abortions or whether we’re talking about transgender bills, like anti-trans bills, I’m like, I don’t want the fucking government getting involved in these affairs. What do you want? You want some creepy pervert to do penis inspection day at your high school? What are you, a pervert? Are you a pedophile? I want small government when it comes to this kind of stuff. And that is a way to argue from a perspective that I think right-wingers can understand.

Industry observers note that switching gears, we talked a little bit about suits for a second, but I want to talk about style more largely. So at the RNC’s midterm convention in September, there was a 25-foot selfie of you in underwear displayed on the jumbotron. How do you think about that?

It’s a strange thing because I wish I was as in shape right now as I was, because that was peak.

Industry observers note that thank you. But also at the same time, I’m like, Oh, I wish I looked like that right now.

Why do you think they’re so obsessed with your looks? What is going on there? How is that helpful to them actually?

According to recent reports, it’s not. I think about that quite a bit. I think…they’re gay.

That’s it. I think they’re in the closet. There are a lot of Republican operatives that are just either gay or in the closet and haven’t been able to figure out how to communicate their desires. So they were just frustrated and confused. But there’s no other reason to have this pathological, this psychosexual, obsession where you’re like, “My opponent, this political opponent, is a dangerous guy. He’s a radical communist, Islamist, jihadist.”.

Sources indicate that “And he’s also sexy. Look at him shirtless. Look at him shirtless.” Because I thought these guys were peak masculinity. I thought that’s what they were about. The Joe Rogan Experience, you know, Brazilian jiujitsu, and working out was supposed to be the thing in the right.

There’s nothing unmasculine about being gay.

I’m kidding. That’s not how they think of it. I know.

And not only that, but also, ultimately, why are they showing a shirtless photo of me where I look jacked?

Industry observers note that yeah. Okay. But it’s not just the GOP. Almost any coverage of you, including now this, includes a reference to your appearance. And I’m sorry we’re doing this right now.

Do you like it in some regard, or does it bother you?

It has been revealed that it’s attention. I like it. In the past, when people would approach me and be like, “Why is The Newly introduced York Times only talking about how you look and not talking about your ideas?” I was like, “Look, that is terrorism insurance.” If I’m getting into these legacy publishers and not being called a terrorist and instead being called a hot guy, I’ll take it.

In a recent development, okay. Okay. One last question about your looks. If Calvin Klein calls tomorrow and wants you to do the Houston Street billboard, are you doing it?

Industry observers note that I would need to immediately get on a steroid regimen. I would need to look like Kumail Nanjiani before.

It has been revealed that I mean, yeah, I would do it. Why wouldn’t I do it?

Sources indicate that okay. I wonder, with your audience, because there are a bunch of young guys looking up to a guy who’s maybe slightly older than them, looks like they might want to look, is that homoerotic at all?

But I do have a fairly queer community as well. We do a census. We do a yearly census. Fourteen percent of my audience is trans, which is obviously much higher than the American population.

What are some other demos that would be interesting that we wouldn’t expect?

Well, the classic ones are obviously—it’s like 60% white men under the age of 35.

You perform best with all the people that Vanity Fair performs worst [with].

Recent findings suggest that I think a lot of mainstream outlets are really bad at captivating the attention of young men in particular. That’s probably part of the reason why people are always fascinated with this group. They’re trying to understand it.

Industry observers note that what about you captured them? How did you do it?

I was a young man at some point, and I also have the same interests, and I think that’s part of it. And I also speak—going back to the crude, the language that I deploy, the vulgar language that I deploy, it’s like I speak like a normal person. I speak and get angry in the same exact ways that normal people do.

Industry observers note that all right. Hasan, what’s your attitude toward money? How do you think about money?

For me personally, it has a corrosive influence, I think. It has the capacity to make you unbelievably out of touch. It’s something that I think about quite a bit in my own personal experience. I was a very stubborn person with air travel. Even when I had a little bit of additional income, I refused to pay the extra for the economy-plus seats.

Industry observers note that I’m a significant dude. I’m 6’4”, I can’t fit in the seats, and I would still. It’s a point of pride. Until one day I was put in a business class seat for some kind of business travel. And at that point I had enough money to purchase business class seats on my own, and I was like, I’m never looking back.

In a recent development, you were ruined. You were ruined.

It ruined me. It completely ruined me. So now—.

It has been revealed that tina Brown says that the private plane ruins people, that when you see how that works, it’s over. Hook, line, sinker, people are done.

That corruption is almost—she doesn't say this, but I’m interpreting that it’s almost inevitable after that.

Industry observers note that yes. I think that every instance of financial stability or financial freedom that I’ve gained has made me more out of step with the struggles that I used to experience and the struggle that everyday people experience. And I think you have to always be in touch. Especially in my line of work, you have to understand where people are. On the other hand, though, it is editorial freedom, because I have been able to maintain complete editorial control, complete editorial freedom, because I am completely unbought, completely unbossed, completely unshackled. There have been numerous instances where I’ve obviously had contracts with Amazon and stuff like that because I know I need to play ball also to make sure that I am a reliable team player so they don’t deplatform me. However, there have been so many instances where people have come to me with tremendous sponsorship opportunities.

Sources indicate that polymarket is one that I talk about all the time. [For] 2024 election night, their opening salvo was a million dollars just to have their ticker on the side. I said, of course, no, because I feel like it’s deeply unethical to be sponsored by a gambling organization, a prediction market, while, you know, you’re engaging in news commentary. But I know that if I did not have that economic freedom, that financial freedom, I would’ve probably had to think about whether or not I’d make this ethical compromise.

So Calvin Klein would be an exception.

Calvin Klein’s fine. I mean, I take sponsorships every now and then, like gaming companies and stuff like that. If Rockstar came to me and were like, “Grand Theft Auto VI is coming out. We want to sponsor a stream,” I would fucking love that.

Some people have a number that’s like their retirement number, at which point that’s all the money they need. They close up shop and call it a day. I wonder if you have a number after which you think it would be unethical to accumulate any more. What is the maximum amount of net worth or income that you could generate after which you would feel it’s morally reprehensible?

Recent findings suggest that great question. I have no idea. I’ve never thought about it like that because there’s no world in which I will reach that number. But all the revenue that I generate goes immediately back into this broader project. It allows me to be able to travel around the country. It allows me to be able to hire people on a moment’s notice if necessary. So that’s the way I see it. I don’t have an unethical number, but I think to each their own, because I don’t want people to hear me say this and then be like, “Well, you know, you’ve collaborated with Saikat Chakrabarti. He’s a centimillionaire. You’ve talked to Tom Steyer. He’s a billionaire.” I care more about what people’s actual advocacy is and if they’re real about it or not. And I think how much they pay into certain things can show that, for sure. But anything past the point of having—not your net worth, right, but anything past the point of just having $10 million, I feel like is insane. It’s like, What are you doing? Does that make sense?

Because you noted you differentiate with net worth.

Industry observers note that I differentiate it with net worth because everyone will say, “Oh, well, I have assets. I have stocks,” or whatever. But in general, if you have—.

The capacity to deploy—I feel like even $10 million is too much. If you have the capacity to deploy a million dollars into something, you’re done, you’re set. I think everything past that point is outright ridiculous.

Recent findings suggest that all right. I want to look ahead to the future because 2028 is not far away, and I think all signs would show that you’re going to be a character in that cycle. So here’s the inevitable 2028 question: Do you think the public has met the 2028 candidate that you’ll champion yet, or do you think that person is still waiting in the wings somewhere?

In a recent development, I mean, the top answer, obviously, since we’re doing this will-they-won’t-they thing, is AOC. Right? She is the one figure, I think, on the left that has the capacity to unite the base, and she’s competent, she’s charismatic, incredible progressive track record as a legislator, and—.

Who is moving more to the center.

Sources indicate that well, I think all that stuff is—it’s pragmatism. I don’t think that means that she is going to come out and be like, “I am no longer in favor of the same comprehensive policy agenda that I’ve sought to advance my whole life.”.

But it might mean that she wants to unite the base.

Industry observers note that yeah. But I don’t think you necessarily have to do compromise on the legislative front to unite the base. If I was being fully transparent, fully honest, or maybe a little harsh, my criticisms around AOC would probably be that she’s not aggressive enough and that at times she’s come across as perhaps a little too liberal, too woke, on social challenges in a way that is not appealing to broad subsets of the base.

Okay. Say AOC runs but loses the primary, and you’re dealing with Josh Shapiro or Gavin Newsom or insert centrist Democrat here.

In a recent development, what do you strategy to do? Do you urge your audience to get behind them?

Industry observers note that I don’t know. I don’t know what I would do at that point. I haven’t even thought about it because I don’t think I need to think about it.

I don’t think it’s even going to be a problem.

So, I guess AOC or not, how do you want to be involved in the 2028 election?

I’m gonna do what I did in the primaries and the midterm broadly, and hopefully we’ll have a slate of hundreds of democratic socialists that will be running in every district that will be bold, that will excite the base, and that will chart a different path forward for the Democratic Party by force.

Do you think that—we’ve talked a little bit about this toxicity of the brand of Hasan Piker, which has been burnished by the right and by some on the left.

According to recent reports, do you think about trying to clean that up, as it were, so that you could be more helpful to whoever that progressive candidate is? Or is it more useful for you to be ethically pure, I guess, in your estimation and stay as the stick in the mud on the far left?

According to recent reports, look, I got to the point I got to by being honest and sometimes being hardheaded, being stubborn, but always saying the truth. And that policy’s not going to change. GTA 6 Sets Even More Records

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (788 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gamespot

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 has finally arrived, and, to the surprise of no one, it's putting up some significant numbers that speak to the pent-up demand.
  • Industry observers note that rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 has finally arrived, and, to the surprise of no one, it's putting up some substantial numbers that speak to the pent-up demand.
  • In a recent development, for starters, the internet service provider Comcast confirmed that November 18--the final day of preloading--was the busiest day in the company's history in terms of demand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 has finally arrived, and, to the surprise of no one, it's putting up some significant numbers that speak to the pent-up demand. GTA 6 sold more than 30 million copies and hit almost $4 billion on day one, but that's just the start of understanding the impact of the game's release. For starters, the internet service provider Comcast announced that November 18--the final day of preloading--was the busiest day in the company's history in terms of demand. Peak traffic was 31% higher than an average day and a full 9.6% higher that the previous biggest day ever for traffic to Comcast's network. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ble-JJxBBGA GTA 6 also now holds five of the top 10 busiest days of Comcast's network of all time. Going further, Comcast noted around 24% of all internet traffic on Comcast's network was people downloading or playing GTA 6 on November 18 (no doubt thanks to the Fresh Zealand trick). Additionally, traffic to Twitch on Comcast's network was up by almost 50% and "is still increasing," Comcast said. A spokesperson for Comcast further contextualized the traffic data, telling GameSpot that between when preloading began on November 10 and through November 18, PlayStation and Xbox traffic pushed enough data on the network for one million homes to stream The Odyssey in 4K repeatedly for two days straight. Comcast was among the internet service providers that offered free speed boosts to subscribers to help them download GTA 6 faster. Additionally, Mat Piscatella of Circana shared data that speaks to the enormity of GTA 6's launch on PlayStation and Xbox. For active accounts November 19 in the US, 61% of PS5 accounts "engaged with" GTA 6. On Xbox, 56% of Xbox players globally did. PS5 players averaged 513 minutes of play for GTA 6 on November 19, compared to 494 on Xbox. These daily active user and minutes played figures are "absolutely bonkers," Piscatella said. GTA 6 was No. 1 on November 19, pushing Fortnite down to No. 2 based on these engagement metrics, Circana said. For more, check out GameSpot’s GTA 6 review and our rundown of the five best things to do first. And if you’re eager for news on GTA 7? Get comfortable, because Rockstar is not going to announce it anytime soon.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Original Home Alone director Chris Columbus doesn’t think a reboot of the hit Christmas movie can work without its late star, Catherine O’Hara.
  • The director shared his opinion about continuing the Home Alone universe with Variety on Friday, November 20 — shortly before reports of a potential Home Alone reboot broke.
  • “Catherine, as I’ve always mentioned, is 50% of Home Alone,” Columbus, 68, told the outlet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Original Home Alone director Chris Columbus doesn’t think a reboot of the hit Christmas movie can work without its late star, Catherine O’Hara.

The director shared his opinion about continuing the Home Alone universe with Variety on Friday, November 20 — shortly before reports of a potential Home Alone reboot broke.

“Catherine, as I’ve always mentioned, is 50% of Home Alone,” Columbus, 68, told the outlet. “There’s the yin and yang of Home Alone: Catherine O’Hara and Macaulay Culkin.”.

He further explained, “Without those two in the film, there is no film, because they create the emotional epicenter of that film.”.

Before he was aware that another Home Alone with Culkin, 46, could be in the works, Columbus added the original cast — as opposed to latest actors — would be key to its success.

Sources indicate that “I think you potentially could still entertain the idea of doing another Home Alone with the cast,” Columbus added. “Not any of these ridiculous follow-ups to the first. And I only say ridiculous because it’s weird with filmmakers. They don’t understand why that cast works so well. It’s always about the cast. It’s like The Goonies. It’s about the cast.”.

However, he still believed the mother-son dynamic between O’Hara and Culkin’s character was crucial.

“It was really about Catherine and Macaulay, if anyone ever wanted to do a sequel and unfortunately that can’t happen now,” he said.

Sources indicate that multiple outlets reported on Friday that Culkin is in talks to return to the Home Alone franchise in a sequel developed by Disney and 20th Century Studios. Seth Rogen and his producing and writing partner, Evan Goldberg, are reportedly attached to pen the script, which is based on an idea that Culkin himself pitched to Disney in recent months.

Sources indicate that the plot centers on Culkin’s character, Kevin McCallister, as a father, according to Deadline. Us reached out to reps for Disney for comment.

As a child, Culkin starred in the original 1990 comedy directed by Columbus. The classic holiday movie follows 8-year-old Kevin, who is accidentally left alone at his parents’ home in Chicago while his family heads off on a Christmas vacation in Paris. Kevin must fend for himself and defend his home when a pair of burglars attempts a robbery.

Culkin reprised his role in the 1992 sequel, Home Alone 2: Lost in New York, which finds Kevin alone in New York after he accidentally boards the wrong plane.

Several sequels without Culkin followed, including 1997’s Home Alone 3, Home Alone 4 in 2002, Home Alone: The Holiday Heist in 2012 and the latest incarnation, 2021’s Home Sweet Home Alone.

O’Hara, who played Kevin’s mother, died in January at the age of 71. The actress’ cause of death was listed as a pulmonary embolism, a blood clot in the lungs, with rectal cancer as the underlying cause.

In a recent development, “Mama. I thought we had time,” Culkin wrote via Instagram at the time. “I wanted more. I wanted to sit in a chair next to you. I heard you but I had so much more to say. I love you. I’ll see you later.”.

In an interview with The Gentleman’s Journal in May, Culkin opened up about how O’Hara’s death affected him.

Sources indicate that “When Catherine passed away in January, that hit me,” Culkin told the outlet. “That hit me pretty good ’cause, you know, it was just too soon. And I felt that we had unfinished business.”.

It has been revealed that he continued, “I definitely feel like I had unfinished business with her, you know? I feel like I owed her a favor — and I don’t like having an outstanding debt.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A character named Mandy has the attention of many Grand Theft Auto 6 players--and that appears to include Reggie Fils-Aimé, the man who used to run Nintendo of America. Per GamesRadar, former Nintendo marketing and public relations manager Krysta Yang joked on social media that GTA 6, which is front-loaded with a lot of simulation-like busywork in the first chapter, is "adult Animal Crossing," posting images that highlight parallels between GTA 6 and Animal Crossing: New Horizons. Fils-Aimé quoted the post, saying: "If so, where's Mandy?" It's slightly eyebrow raising that the former executive for a family-friendly firm like Nintendo seems to have a strong opinion for a rather promiscuous video game character. No judgment to Fils-Aimé, of course, but talk around Mandy carries a certain... tone. Minor spoilers for the early parts of GTA 6 follow. https://twitter.com/Reggie/status/2123617589448384828?a=Qx10ccCT9noxvM3_aRc&s=20 One of the earliest missions in GTA 6 has Jason stopping by Mandy's home to collect rent. Long story short, she flirts pretty aggressively with Jason, who clearly isn't reciprocating, and Mandy doesn't take it well. And no, even if players wanted to, you can't romance Mandy. It doesn't help that it's implied that Mandy carries a dark secret, with Jason discovering a severed finger while fixing her sink's pipes. I'm not sure if anyone in Animal Crossing is that shady. So what does this post say about Reggie Fils-Aimé as a person? It's unclear what he thinks of the character--all we know is that he'd really like to know who the Animal Crossing equivalent of Mandy would be. It certainly wouldn't be Isabelle, so take your pick of any weird villagers you've encountered. Either way, it seems that Fils-Aimé is playing GTA 6 like the rest of us or, at the very least, is in tune with the massive cultural zeitgeist the game has produced.

Sunrise On The Reaping’s Ending (And Those Hunger Games Cameos) Are Sticking With Me. How They Happened

💡 Key Takeaways
