📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that VSCO today released Studio Pro Desktop, its first native photo editor for Mac, bringing many of the tech giant’s familiar editing tools to macOS, alongside upcoming features aimed at photographers working with large numbers of images. Here are the details.

Professional and amateur photographers just got a fresh alternative for editing and managing their photos on Mac with the release of VSCO Studio Pro, a native macOS app that brings the firm’s popular editing tools to the desktop for the first time.

More than that, VSCO Studio Pro integrates with the tech giant’s broader ecosystem of photography tools, allowing owners to manage their workflow from importing and editing photos to delivering finished images to clients through VSCO Galleries, without having to manually export and upload them to another app.

It also supports keyboard shortcuts similar to those found in other popular photo editors, making it easier for photographers familiar with those apps to get started.

Here’s Eric Wittman, CEO of VSCO, on today’s launch:.

“Photographers deserve tools built around how they actually work. […] 75% of VSCO Pro members have used our presets in the last six months. Now those looks live on the desktop, with one connected workflow from camera to client delivery and nothing getting in the way.

Recent findings suggest that the first thing consumers will notice, and then continue to notice when using VSCO Studio Pro, is how fast it is. From changing the grid size, to sorting images, to applying presets by rolling the cursor over each of the 200+ presets, pretty much everything about VSCO Studio Pro feels as real-time and instant as it can be when dealing with large numbers of images.

According to recent reports, as for importing photos, VSCO Studio Pro supports Apple Photos, local folders, SD cards, and external drives, and offers RAW compatibility with more than 800 cameras from 20 brands. People can also choose whether to work with files in their original location or copy them elsewhere.

Under the hood, VSCO Studio Pro Desktop combines Apple’s Core Image RAW processing with the firm’s own Reflex image processing engine, which handles presets and editing adjustments.

Batch editing in VSCO Studio Pro Desktop can handle anywhere from two to 500 images at once, which is great for rapidly applying the same preset or film-inspired look (including Kodak Portra, Kodachrome, Fujifilm Velvia, and Kodak Tri-X), or making adjustments to an entire set of photos simultaneously, with changes appearing across all selected images in real time.

And speaking of presets, VSCO Studio Pro packs an exclusive one called IOE1 Pro, developed with photographer Joe Greer. IOE1 Pro, as well as VSCO’s other presets, allow users to adjust the strength, color, tone, and contrast, further helping them fine-tune each look to their liking.

VSCO Studio Pro’s editing tools include the usual suspects photographers might expect from photo editing software, including exposure, contrast, fade, highlights, shadows, whites, blacks, skin tone, temperature, tint, hue, saturation, lightness, sharpening, clarity, vignetting, and grain adjustments for strength, size, and color.

VSCO is also working to expand its toolset to include bloom and halation effects, curves, masks, and a remove tool for users looking for more control over their edits and to make more precise, localized adjustments to their images.

Also in the works are new organizational features, including projects for managing groups of photos, as well as culling tools that will allow users to rate images with stars and mark them as accepted or rejected, making it easier to sort through large photo collections.

Once users are happy with their adjustments, they can export their photos individually or in batches, choosing the file name, format, resolution, and compression quality. VSCO Studio Pro also offers resizing presets for web, social media, and client delivery, as well as the option to save the finished images to a folder of their choice.

And speaking of client delivery, people can publish their edited photos directly to VSCO Galleries, allowing them to share full-resolution images without having to export them and upload them separately elsewhere.

According to recent reports, VSCO Studio Pro Desktop is available today as a free download for Apple Silicon Macs, with full feature access requiring a VSCO Pro membership, starting at $4.99 per month or $59.99 per year, or a VSCO One membership. You can see it in action below:.

#39885. Latest Update: Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1286 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1286 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font.
  • According to recent reports, at this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt.
  • Recent findings suggest that to borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”.

According to recent reports, at this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

Recent findings suggest that to borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

The problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

It has been revealed that for example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

Those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT demonstrated me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

While most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”.

Recent findings suggest that the reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

Sources indicate that this pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic.".

If there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

One of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

Industry observers note that in every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

Recent findings suggest that the generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

This is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

To a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

Recent findings suggest that that means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

Starting today, the Gemini app’s “tasks” feature, previously known as Spark, is now available for free users after requiring AI Pro in the past.

Google previously referred to this capability as a 24/7 personal agent before integrating directly into the main Gemini app experience in October. Above the prompt box on mobile (or below on the web), you’ll see “Chat” and “Task.” The first option is the existing chatbot, while the latter lets you “hand off even more tasks to Gemini.”.

With tasks, Google’s “goal is for Gemini to save you time and money.” Google shared use cases like:.

With today’s announcement, Google is emphasizing that “Gemini is your best choice as a personal assistant because [your emails, calendar, passwords, photos, files, and payment cards] already lives at Google securely, and you don’t have to send it elsewhere.”.

Behind the scenes, Gemini tasks work in your own “hardware-isolated virtual machine” that’s sandboxed and has protections against prompt injection, while leveraging Google Safe Browsing when browsing the web.

Other safety features include having you confirm purchases and asking “clarifying questions if an instruction is ambiguous.”.

Powered by the new Hydrogen model, free Gemini tasks are available in the US, Japan, Korea, Canada, Australia, and India.

This week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

In a recent development, you can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

Would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

According to recent reports, in the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.).

It has been revealed that in the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

Here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart quickly led to women posting the waist heart.

In a recent development, okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

As if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber reveals up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?".

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood.".

According to recent reports, [Editor’s note: This review was originally published on October 2, 2026 during the 2026 Fresh York Film Festival. Janus Film will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, November 20.].

Paul Thomas Anderson‘s eye for vivifying music onscreen dates back to the late 1990s when, after “Boogie Nights,” he made Technicolor mini-masterpiece music videos with his ex-girlfriend Fiona Apple — or made a San Fernando Valley-sized shrine to Aimee Mann with his third feature, “Magnolia.” Since then, he’s kicked around with HAIM while turning one third of its Los Angelino triumvirate, Alana Haim, into a screen actress. He’s shot for Radiohead and made a regular collaboration with band member Jonny Greenwood to create some of the 21st century’s most memorable scores. Many young cinephiles now associate the mischievously lilty notes of “Phantom Thread” with the poison promise of latest love and obsessive creation. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

Last December, PTA teamed up with Geese frontman Cameron Winter to film, while operating his own Panavision camera, his solo stage performance at Carnegie Hall, running through sparse piano arrangements of tracks off his solo album, “Heavy Metal.” The result, a 72-minute film now being distributed roadshow-style by Janus Films before inevitably living on the Criterion Collection, is a stunning arrangement of its own: a deeply achey, sincere but never cloyingly earnest concert movie that’s tender to the point of frailty. (Benny Safdie counts as a co-producer, and the film’s scratchy Upcoming York quality and setting can’t help but have his imprint.).

It has been revealed that the matted-hair, lithe Winter can seem a bit uncomfortable in his own skin in the public eye, as he did onstage ahead of “Cameron Winter at Carnegie” at its Fresh York Film Festival world premiere at Alice Tully Hall. But on the piano, laser-beamed into his songcraft, he’s quietly electrified, at seemingly at peace as his tenorous vocal glissando and nimble fingerwork on the piano produce shiveringly tender folk ballads that echo Harry Nilsson and Van Morrison. (The usual comparisons to Tom Waits and Rufus Wainright are right, too, but Winter is his own strange thing.) If you weren’t previously sold on the wily Winter antic rock chaos of Geese — rapidly becoming one of the most popular contemporary art rock bands of these times — you’re about to. Paul Thomas Anderson has created a rhapsodic shrine to the man that is nonetheless ballad-sized in its emotional scale.

Industry observers note that winter, in December, played and sang to a sold-out crowd of more than 2,700 at the stately cultural temple that is Carnegie Hall, and this film can at times feel like a religious experience, an incantation, a lonely vigil. The singer/songwriter was 23 at the time of the performance, one year older than Bob Dylan when he headlined Carnegie Hall, and similarly at the precipice of major fame. Fixed on a mobile rig that will at times careen and whoosh across the stage when not otherwise holding on Winter, Anderson’s camera catches the expressionism and chiaroscuro of stage lights illuminating and fading off the singer’s face.

The result is hynoptic, a concert film up there with “Stop Making Sense” but for introverts. Songs like the popular single “$0” acquire an even more wrenchingly somber quality as a lovelorn protagonist rues being exploited by a relationship (“You’re making me feel like a dollar in your hand / You’re making me feel like I’m a zero dollar man”). Stripped of production, his indie hit “Love Takes Miles” plays even better. While many of the songs sort of hover in the same key and bleed into one another, that makes for an all the more transfixing experience. The lack of an interstitial anything save for a sweet prologue and moving coda make for experience also that’s immersive, deep, and the kind whose truth you can feel somewhere in your body even if you can’t quite articulate it.

“Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall premiered at the Newly introduced York Film Festival. Janus Films will release it in theaters starting November 20.

#39876. Deterministic Simulation Testing Is for Everyone

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1157 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdata ↗ Open Full Page

Deterministic Simulation Testing Is for Everyone

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1157 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdata

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Deterministic Simulation Testing is often seen as a technique just for distributed systems.
  • Why do we use automated testing when building software?
  • We test because we want to find complications internally and not have them be found for us by customers (who may not even report them at all).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Deterministic Simulation Testing is often seen as a technique just for distributed systems. I argue that it's a testing technique for everyone and all applications.

Why do we use automated testing when building software?

We test because we want to find complications internally and not have them be found for us by customers (who may not even report them at all).

We do this reactively; when an implementation bug is found, a failing test we think corresponds to the bug is written, and the system is changed to make the test pass. If the bug can no longer be reproduced, we have proven to ourselves that the test corresponds to the bug, and we keep the test to guard against further regressions.

We can also do this defensively; predicting where and what the bugs might be, and using tests as guardrails ensuring they do not occur in development.

We test because we are plagued with self-doubt.

Doubting every development decision we make is exhausting. Can this feature be added? Can this dependency be removed? Can these modules be re-arranged? Can this all be done without breaking what we already have? Second guessing brings decision fatigue. Doubt kills productivity. If we are confident the machine is checking this for us, then our confidence grows.

We test because we ought to test, in the same way a small child brushes their teeth - they may not see the point but they know someone else will make their lives hard if they don't.

According to recent reports, in Test-Driven Development, each bit of code must be preceded by a failing test. Tests are written under TDD because without them nothing at all can be written. It follows that these tests tend to be numerous, brittle, numerous, limited in utility and numerous. Obligation is an external pressure, and if that external pressure is gone (i.e., the senior TDD champion leaves the organization), the obligation leaves with it.

I see limited utility in testing processes driven by obligation.

The utility of a test can be evaluated across three dimensions.

Tests have a certain scope. This scope may be anything from an individual function to an entire program. The greater the scope, the more interesting the properties we can reason about. If the scope is large enough, properties start corresponding to the requirements; that is we can test things relevant to the real world.

A test is run many times. A non-deterministic or "flaky" test can produce different results even when the SUT, test logic, and test seed remain the same. Such tests are incredibly frustrating for the developer - how can they tell if a bug is fixed if their tests don't produce consistent results?

According to recent reports, if a test is deterministic, then the same code with the same test will return the same failure. Always.

It has been revealed that in some tests, specific examples are thought up by the programmer, and specific states or responses are tested for. In others the inputs to the SUT are described declaratively and generated randomly, so that each run generates multiple different examples. This lets us explore a lot more of the state space. Let's call these tests thorough.

Different testing approaches ask different kinds of questions:.

The different testing approaches can be analysed according to the criteria discussed above:.

It has been revealed that in the above analysis Deterministic Simulation Testing (henceforth DST) stands out. So how does it work? In short they combine a simulated environment with a deterministic machine. Let's look at these terms in detail.

The whole program, hence the SUT, is a deterministic machine. This means it's single-threaded (or at least deterministically scheduled) and does not make direct IO calls; so you're left with input-driven deterministic state machines, making the same state transitions for the same inputs every single time.

If you're interested in how to do this, see my previous article on designing programs around a deterministic core .

According to recent reports, the environment is simulated. This includes all relevant real world phenomena that are shared with the deterministic machine, for example:.

Recent findings suggest that simulating the environment turns a source of non-determinism into something deterministic. Given the same seed, the simulated environment always produces the same outputs. It also allows you to dial up the chaos: weird inputs, failures and coincidences that will "never happen" can all be dialled up. A good simulation is an exercise in amplifying the deviousness of those parts of the environment we cannot control.

It has been revealed that typically the test is its own executable. A seed is provided, and a test loop is run using the simulated environment and the deterministic machine, checking that properties hold each loop. If a property does not hold the loop exits and the executable returns the failing seed. This makes errors reproducible.

Some DST implementations act like a game loop, using ticks to simulate time; just as an "in-game" day might take 24 minutes of real time to represent 24 hours of game time, a simulation test might take 1 month of sim time but complete in one hour of real time. Others model progression through the test as distinct events, jumping from one to the next. In either case, because all network and storage delay is simulated, the test never has to truly wait, and things can progress much faster than they would under a real environment. This minimises "time to bug", in effect compressing time, and surfacing problems far more quickly than it would ever take them to appear naturally in production.

When people think of DST, a few products come to mind: Dropbox, FoundationDB, TigerBeetle, Turso; all very clever systems engineering products made by people who are essentially wizards.

But conceptually, all software programs have an environment and a machine. If you make the machine deterministic, and you define an interface for the environment so it can be simulated, then you can do DST.

Here are some examples of how DST can apply to different kinds of software:.

It has been revealed that DST is not driven by obligation, it does not plague developers with doubt; it lets them build without fear, by finding as many bugs in development as possible. Development is the best place to find bugs.

DST improves architecture by maximising the amount of code in the deterministic context, and carefully controlling exposure to the environment.

DST is under your control; you do not have to rely on someone else to simulate the entire world for you - just the environment you care about.

In a recent development, my goal in this article is not to dissuade you from unit tests, property-based tests, or any other testing technique. My goal is to persuade you that DST is relevant for you and your team. Don't let a technique being associated with one domain stop you from considering using it in yours.

What ‘Digger’ Has in Common with Gary Oldman’s Winston Churchill and Charlize Theron’s Megyn Kelly

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (926 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tom Cruise‘s performance in Alejandro González Iñárritu‘s “Digger” is one of the boldest and most entertaining of the actor’s career, as he suppresses not only his usual movie star charisma but his entire way of walking and talking to play paunchy, aging oil tycoon Digger Rockwell.
  • To aid in his complete transformation, Cruise called on one of the best prosthetic designers in the business, Kazu Hiro.
  • It has been revealed that “Alejandro is an amazing director, and he has lots of ideas,” Hiro told IndieWire.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tom Cruise‘s performance in Alejandro González Iñárritu‘s “Digger” is one of the boldest and most entertaining of the actor’s career, as he suppresses not only his usual movie star charisma but his entire way of walking and talking to play paunchy, aging oil tycoon Digger Rockwell. Cruise is barely recognizable in the role, which is about as far from heroic characters like Pete “Maverick” Mitchell and Ethan Hunt as Cruise’s Ron Kovic in “Born on the Fourth of July” was from race car driver Cole Trickle almost 40 years ago.

To aid in his complete transformation, Cruise called on one of the best prosthetic designers in the business, Kazu Hiro. Hiro has turned Gary Oldman into Winston Churchill (“The Darkest Hour”), Charlize Theron into Megyn Kelly (“Bombshell”), and Dwayne Johnson into “Smashing Machine” Mark Kerr, but transforming Cruise into Texas oilman Digger Rockwell was a whole fresh task — one made even more challenging by Iñárritu and Cruise’s persistent striving for perfectionism, and constant eagerness to try new approaches. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

It has been revealed that “Alejandro is an amazing director, and he has lots of ideas,” Hiro told IndieWire. “Every day he comes in with a upcoming idea, and we have to come up with an answer for how to achieve it. And Tom is really professional, and expects everybody else to be at that same level, ready for any situation. After the first day of testing, I learned that I had to stay flexible to respond to whatever they wanted.”.

To that end, Hiro created modular prosthetics whose parts could easily be swapped out and moved around, so that Cruise and Iñárritu could constantly try newly introduced looks. “Sometimes with heavy makeup, you can’t change it,” Hiro said. “I created prosthetics that could be mixed, so we could make new designs on the spot — try this forehead with these cheeks and this nose, then change it.” Creating Cruise’s look was a constantly evolving process throughout the long prep period. “We didn’t have a clear answer until the end of rehearsal.”.

According to recent reports, hiro’s mandate at the beginning was a bit open-ended, which gave him room for artistic exploration but also made it difficult to zero in on a precise look. “Alejandro mentioned the character was 76 years old and an oil tycoon,” Hiro said. “He also said he didn’t want the character to look like Tom, but he still wanted to see Tom in the character.” To try to find a concrete image for Digger Rockwell, Hiro immersed himself in research.

“I researched real oil tycoons and how they aged and what kinds of lifestyles they had,” Hiro said. “Those lifestyles affect how they age.” As Hiro did more and more research, however, he realized that there was no one look that defined the entire profession he was trying to represent. “Everybody looked so different, so in the end I relied more on the storyline and how this particular character behaved.” The idea, in keeping with the slightly heightened style of the film as a whole, was to exaggerate Cruise’s features but keep the character realistic.

It has been revealed that hiro began with a 3D scan and life cast of Cruise, which he used to sculpt his designs. His paramount concern was allowing the actor to be as expressive as possible under the makeup. “The important part is to make the prosthetic very soft so he can move,” Hiro said, noting that three weeks before shooting, Iñárritu called with a significant change. “He decided that Digger should be 65, not 76, so I swiftly made a new design. Tom is around that age, but he looks much younger than a normal 65. Under his eye was exposed and the rest of the face was covered, but I made it thin to give him freedom.”.

In a recent development, in addition to Digger’s face, Hiro was also tasked with creating an upper body for an early scene in which Cruise would be seen stripped down to his pajama pants. The body prosthetic was intended only for that one scene, with a lighter bodysuit created for the rest of the movie. “We made a light version of the padding for under the costume, because we don’t need to see the skin after that first scene,” Hiro stated. “For the first scene we made a silicone prosthetic that was a lot heavier — the body padding was around 10 pounds, but the silicone was 40 or 50.”.

During one of Cruise’s costume fittings, he told Hiro he wanted to feel the weight of the silicone throughout production. “He tried the body prosthetic on and stated, ‘I like this, I want to wear it every day,'” Hiro said. “I told him it would be really heavy and hot, but he said he was training and would be fine.” Since gluing the body prosthetic on every day would be extremely time-consuming, Hiro created a strong spandex foundation and glued the prosthetic to it so Cruise could slip it on each day.

According to recent reports, “He wore that for the whole film,” Hiro said. “One time he said, ‘This is so heavy, it’s really hard on my back.’ I thought, ‘Okay, you asked for it,’ but he went through with it and finished the film, so that was amazing.”.

Instead, Pharaoh captured both Rogue and Don, leaving the two in a precarious Saw-like situation. It might seem like a step back, but it’s really a step closer to taking down the season's Substantial Bad (Don and Rogue working together has proven quite effective so far). However, while Pharaoh might be on their way out when the show returns in January, a more sinister villain remains — and they need to be dealt with.

In a recent development, cammie was again harassed by crank calls from her boss, Marcia, during the opening of 9-1-1: Nashville’s mid-season finale. Few clues have been offered about why Marcia might be so obsessed with bullying Cammie, but no clear explanation has been given. For now, Marcia’s villainy is more sinister than Pharaoh’s — Pharaoh might be murderous and chaotic, and their reasoning hasn't been revealed yet, but at least they have a proposal. With no endgame to her harassment in sight, Marcia's next move is up in the air.

At first glance, Marcia seems like nothing more than a difficult boss. She’s somewhat manipulative. She's incredibly nice to everyone until she suddenly becomes overly critical, berating the 911 operators for being too emotional on calls and threatening to let AI take over their jobs. Then, she targets Cammie by playing the 911 call of her husband’s death in front of everyone. As harsh as that is, it's still "bad boss" territory. However, the revelation that she’s the one prank-calling Cammie turns it into a personal vendetta.

In the second episode she appeared in, Marcia told Cammie that she lost her son to a drunk driver when he was about 12 years old. Between that, the emphasis on not tying up the call center lines, and the harassment of Cammie, it makes one wonder if Cammie was the operator who answered the call about Marcia’s son, but got to it too late to help because the changes she was making weren't fully implemented, and the call was forced to hold. That would make Marcia’s efforts to tear Cammie down make sense, at least.

In a recent development, however, Marcia’s son had to have died at least a couple of years ago, so if she’s been plotting to find a way to become head of the call center solely to make crank calls, that’s wild (and honestly, not a great revenge plot). That leaves the question of where Marcia is headed with all of this, and how far 9-1-1: Nashville season 2 is willing to let her go. If crank calls are just the start, numerous possibilities could follow, from swatting to murder (depending on how dark the show wants to go this season).

The impact of Marcia’s villainy on Cammie, her family, her boyfriend, and the rest of the firefighting family depends on how her harassment evolves next. If she keeps up the crank calls, it will definitely affect Cammie’s mental health; that might even be the point, since, as Cammie’s boss, Marcia keeps saying she's responsible for the employees' mental health and well-being. Cammie’s mental health suffering gives Marcia the perfect opportunity to fire her from the call center, which might be all she’s aiming for.

It’s doubtful, though, that Cammie wouldn’t be back at her job in a few weeks (she’s the steadiest character on the show and 9-1-1: Nashville needs her), but it would create fantastic drama for a few episodes. Of course, if Marcia decides to take things further by putting Cammie actively in harm’s way, the consequences for everyone could be devastating. Doing that would put Marcia in harm’s way, too, though, because it’s safe to say the entire 113 (and Blythe) would come down in full force to protect Cammie.

It has been revealed that that decision would likely end with Marcia behind bars. If 9-1-1: Nashville wants to keep her around long-term, though, she would need to actually have an honest conversation with Cammie. There would be no one better than Cammie to understand what it's like to have a loved one die because 911 didn't immediately answer a call. While that seems like the most reasonable option, Marcia has proven to be entirely unreasonable, so where her actions lead in the future remains to be seen.

It's the sixth installment in the dystopian sci-fi franchise based on Suzanne Collins' bestselling novels, and the second prequel following The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes. That movie was produced on a comparatively modest reported budget of $100 million, and it went on to gross around $360 million worldwide.

This was by far the lowest box-office haul in the franchise's history. The series began with director Gary Ross' original The Hunger Games film, which made nearly $700 million worldwide against a reported budget of under $70 million in 2012 and turned Jennifer Lawrence into a star. It was followed by three direct sequels directed by Francis Lawrence: The Hunger Games: Catching Fire, The Hunger Games: Mockingjay — Part 1, The Hunger Games: Mockingjay — Part 2.

Sources indicate that lawrence also helmed The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, which tells the origin story of the villainous President Coriolanus Snow, and Sunrise on the Reaping, which focuses on the tragic hero Haymitch Abernathy. The character was played by Woody Harrelson in the original films. The upcoming film has received relatively muted praise from critics and is sitting at a 67% score on the aggregator website Rotten Tomatoes, although its audience score is perched at a "Verified Hot" 95%.

Fan appreciation is certainly going a long way in pushing the film past expectations this weekend. Sunrise on the Reaping generated $21 million in Thursday previews, exceeding The Odyssey's preview haul and setting itself up for a domestic debut in the $120 million range. The movie is projected to break past the $200 million mark worldwide by Sunday, potentially recouping its reported $150 million budget in three days flat. Sunrise on the Reaping stars newcomer Joseph Zada in the lead role, along with a celebrated supporting cast including Jesse Plemons, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Glenn Close, and Ralph Fiennes. You can watch the movie in theaters and stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

Taking place in Panem 24 years prior to the original series, this fresh Hunger Games entry focuses on the reaping of the 50th Hunger Games.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The legacy-quel is alive and well, and it only makes sense that a sequel/reboot/reimagining would eventually come for “Home Alone,” Chris Columbus’ 1990 holiday classic starring Macaulay Culkin.

There was buzz that Culkin over the summer pitched an idea to Disney as to where a grown Kevin McAllister would be today after enduring two child abandonments and harassment and attempted murder from bumbling bandits (our interpretation, not necessarily his read on Kevin’s childhood shenanigans and trauma). Disney now seems to have warmed to the idea like a cup of hot cocoa, especially thanks to the two additional names who are working with Culkin on the project: Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch.

Disney’s 20th Century Studios is in early development on a sequel to “Home Alone” that would star Culkin reprising his original role and in which Rogen and Goldberg on behalf of their Point Grey banner would write and produce the film, working with Culkin on his idea, IndieWire has learned.

Things are very, very early days, and any plot details are being kept under wraps for now, and no director is attached at the moment.

According to recent reports, chris Columbus directed the original “Home Alone” and its nearly-as-loved sequel “Home Alone 2: Lost in New York,” and both written by the late great John Hughes. If you can believe it, there have been six “Home Alone” movies in all, with the third one at least released in theaters and doing respectable box office numbers. The others are all TV movies or in the case of the most recent 2021 film “Home Sweet Home Alone,” a Disney+ streaming movie.

Recent findings suggest that the original two films though grossed $477 million and $358 million worldwide, respectively, and the original still gets tons of cable play and finds its way into the Nielsen streaming charts. It makes sense that a more serious sequel with Culkin back in the fold would be welcomed by audiences.

Sadly, “Home Alone” has been back on the minds of audiences of late after the recent passing of Catherine O’Hara, who played Kevin’s mom, and also Tim Curry, who had a small role as a hotel clerk in “Home Alone 2.” Joe Pesci and Daniel Stern as the Wet Bandits are still around, though Pesci has been mostly retired outside of his return in Scorsese’s “The Irishman” back in 2019 and his role in the Pete Davidson Peacock series “Bupkis” in 2023.

Culkin too has had a bit of a resurgence, making a cameo in the most recent season of “Fallout” and doing a voice in Disney’s “Zootopia 2.”.

#39867. Breaking: How I made a custom game engine for Satelital

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2927 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Spectralorbit ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: How I made a custom game engine for Satelital

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2927 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spectralorbit

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, seven years ago I decided to start learning how to make a game from scratch.
  • As a solo developer, I decided to start this project from scratch.
  • Now that I've finally managed to release the game, I think it's a good moment to share how I built it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, seven years ago I decided to start learning how to make a game from scratch. And last week I released Satelital, a rule-discovery game about learning alien logic.

As a solo developer, I decided to start this project from scratch. My motivation was to learn the actual fundamentals behind the technology of videogames. This meant I had to build most of the tools I would need myself, including the game engine, renderer, puzzles, editors, UX, design, art and music.

Now that I've finally managed to release the game, I think it's a good moment to share how I built it.

The main reason I got into programming was the idea of eventually working on games. I spent many years working on web and building mobile apps. It was fun, but I felt like I wasn't going in the direction I really wanted to.

So one day, after listening to every Jonathan Blow talk I could find and playing too much The Witness, I decided to finally give it a try.

In a recent development, I spent many days and countless hours looking for the best tool I could use to make a game, but nothing left me satisfied. The closest I got to having fun with gamedev was with the LÖVE framework making a few jam games. But even with that, it felt quite limiting to not really know what was happening behind the graphics I somehow managed to animate on my screen.

I remember hearing about shaders and parallel programming. The concept always felt very arcane and mysterious to me, but now writing them is the thing I enjoy the most while coding.

I finally decided to jump into the swimming pool and actually learn C⁠+⁠+. I had to learn how to manage memory and how not to shoot myself in the foot with the wrong tools. I started using SDL2 while trying to use the C⁠+⁠+ standard library as little as possible.

Before getting too deep into the engine, I actually finished a prototype of the puzzles not long after learning how to draw some simple graphics with C⁠+⁠+. It had very early versions of four kinds of puzzles that mostly survived until the final game. It was made entirely with SDL2, but I soon realised that if I wanted more interesting graphics, I would need to use shaders and decided to switch to OpenGL.

According to recent reports, with the help of LearnOpenGL I swiftly had a triangle on the screen. From there, learning things like lighting, tonemapping, normal maps, shader effects and everything else opened up a whole new way of looking at computers for me. Before, my idea of how a computer actually draws to the screen was quite naive. When I started learning graphics I just wanted to be able to manually change the color of each pixel individually, but in the end the idea of running a program in parallel for every pixel clicked for me.

Sources indicate that one thing that made a huge difference while working on shaders was having code reloading. Before that, I had a complex system that stored constant values in config files, which would later get passed through uniforms into shaders. Then a custom development menu would provide some UI to tweak those values at runtime. With that I stopped having to reload and compile everything for every little change I wanted to make.

It worked, but having to maintain all this extra scaffolding was slowing me down. Another unexpected downside of this setup was that, in some cases, the shader compiler couldn't optimize the code as well as it otherwise could, since knowing constant values ahead of time helps it make better decisions.

Sources indicate that having shader reloading made a huge difference. Being able to change some code, save the file and immediately see the result on screen was very useful. Iterating on shaders became much faster and more fun. This was probably my biggest regret about not having it from day one.

For a major part of the development I was using SDL2, mainly to create a window, read input and get a surface to draw on. But it felt wrong to depend on a library that was several times bigger than my entire game just to handle a few seemingly simple tasks. I decided to drop that dependency and make my own platform layer that I could understand and maintain. I wouldn't have to wait for someone else to fix a bug anymore because now I could just change it myself. It wasn't that hard to end up with a single file with a few thousand lines of code that supported both macOS and Windows. I'm now looking forward to working on mobile and console ports, it feels like it might be a fun thing to work on.

In a recent development, at some point during development, compile times were getting longer, so I decided to look into what was going on. I checked where all that time was going, and to my surprise a lot of it was spent compiling standard library things. Stuff like std::function was particularly slow for example.

Sources indicate that eventually I realised that I wasn't actually forced to use the standard library just because it was there, and the subset I needed wasn't that hard to implement myself. It took me a month to replace it with my own base library, but it was so worth it. Not only did compile times get faster, but I also learned how a lot of things I had always taken for granted in other languages actually worked.

Sources indicate that at some point I started looking into Vulkan because I wanted HDR. I couldn't get it working on macOS through OpenGL and I was worried about OpenGL being deprecated in the future. Also I didn't really want to build the whole engine around an API that might become deprecated.

Moving to Vulkan was rough at the beginning. There was so much boilerplate to type and understand. Also, when I started working on the engine, there wasn't much documentation around how to implement a good backend with it. In hindsight, I feel that even though I got a lot of valuable things from tutorials and books, most of them were overcomplicating something that could be much more straightforward. I still have nightmares about trying to resize a window...

Getting Vulkan working on macOS was actually surprisingly easy thanks to MoltenVK. It was nice not having to learn Metal and being able to keep the same codebase on Windows. The engine started out only working on macOS, so I was afraid I'd run into a lot of concerns when porting it to Windows. But I was quite nice to see Vulkan just working the same day I tried it.

My philosophy from day one was to only grow the engine towards exactly what I needed. This was a long solo project, so trying to build a general purpose engine first, without knowing what I needed, would probably have meant never finishing the game. I did waste time on things I thought I would need, but I cut them when I knew I wouldn't be using them. Because I was also learning C/C⁠+⁠+ along the way, I made many coding mistakes but I wasn't afraid of big refactors. Cleaning the codebase helped me bring up my morale.

From the beginning I wanted to avoid making a 3D engine since I knew that might complicate things too much. But after I finished the prototype, I kept learning about shader techniques and effects. So in the end, my goal was to get as close as possible to a 3D look without actually having to load any 3D polygons.

It has been revealed that to do this, I chose an orthographic top-down view so I could just prerender the assets in Blender and then load their albedo, normal and height maps as textures. Having a fixed camera meant I could render all the assets from exactly the same perspective, so they would always fit together properly in the game. Other things that needed to be animated were drawn in the pixel shader using SDFs. The terrain of the planets was too big to be stored entirely in textures, so in most cases I had to procedurally generate them in shaders too.

Since I wanted a 3D look with dynamic lighting, I also needed dynamic shadows. The final approach I settled on was ray marching. With the height map of each prop, I could make them look as if they were actually sitting in a 3D space, even though everything was still rendered in 2D. In the shader I basically march along the direction of the light and sample the height map to figure out where a shadow should be drawn.

Having the height map was also useful for other things. For example, I could use that information to make objects interact with the water in a convincing way. Objects can actually submerge in the ocean instead of looking like flat images drawn on top of it. This is also how the waves can interact with the shore around an island.

Industry observers note that the engine was only one part of making a complete game. I also had to build a custom level editor. I wanted to make it as easy as possible to design and iterate on puzzles, so I integrated an edit mode that allowed me to change puzzles and the enviroment at runtime and see the changes in real time.

It was quite fun to swiftly draw and tweak puzzles directly in the game. It helped me discover so many ideas. After making thousands of puzzles, you start to develop a sense of beauty about how a puzzle should be. Having this editor allowed me to get into the zone. I could spend hours making puzzles without actually thinking about the tool I was using.

In a recent development, alongside the in-game editor I made a custom Blender plugin that could load my level config files into Blender. The game had a file watcher that could detect changes in the baked textures of the 3D models rendered by Blender. But it could also load level data and provide another way to edit. The upside was being able to just use Blender tools like multi-select, but aside from that, it wasn't actually that useful. It was cool to make though, and it's an interesting demo. But just being able to edit things in-game was much better, since you can see how it will actually look in the end. Though having mentioned that, looking at the levels in an actual 3D environment feels quite nice.

Industry observers note that building the game with all these custom tools brought some challenges. They worked on my machine, but when I started playtesting I began to find lots of bugs that were tricky to reproduce. The hardest ones were related to graphics, due to differences in hardware and drivers on machines I didn't have access to. Tools like Vulkan validation layers were quite useful, though they didn't catch everything.

According to recent reports, another thing that was tricky to deal with was shader compatibility. When using GLSL, if you rely heavily on making visual effects with noise related functions, you will find complications with things like sin or pow because the specification doesn't guarantee their precision. So I had to be constantly checking that everything looked the same on as many different hardware configurations as I could find. For a while, I didn't notice that the distribution pattern of my stars looked different across vendors. It looked correct, but I wanted to have the same placement of stars wherever you played to make it feel more like an actual place.

Having good logs to see how the internals of the game were working ended up being very useful. It was essential for me to have them after I released the demo and started getting feedback from customers who were seeing errors I couldn't reproduce. Many of them reported a black screen when trying to open the game for the first time, and these were caused by many different kinds of problems. Sometimes it would be a missing extension, sometimes a third party Vulkan layer injecting code that prevented the frame from being drawn, or some other particular driver issue. Without the logs showing the exact point when the error happened, it would have been almost impossible to fix these bugs without having the actual hardware.

Recent findings suggest that the logs ended up being quite useful for performance. For example, when trying to do optimizations for Intel GPUs, I noticed that some of the biggest shaders were being compiled in a non-optimal way. I basically ran the whole game in just 2 big shaders, one to blend the scene with all the quads, and another pass where I do lighting, shadows and effects like water, where the final normal and height map of the scene are presented. Because these shaders were so big, they couldn't be compiled for SIMD16.

Sources indicate that these integrated Intel GPUs are quite common on laptops, and they can shade 16 pixels at once, but only if everything in the shader fits in a small amount of very fast memory. Because my shaders grew so much and I wasn't even aware that this would be an actual issue, the driver was quietly falling back to shading 8 pixels at a time, making the game run noticeably slower. Once I had this information in the logs, I could see what I needed to trim down. I reduced the number of values I needed to keep around as much as possible, while also avoiding duplicated code caused by things like macros until everything fit again.

In a recent development, during development I was always careful about how demanding the game was, but after switching to a faster computer I started paying less attention to it. It's quite easy to just settle for something that looks good enough and move on to the next thing when you're busy. That's why I started targeting the Steam Deck and aiming for stable 90 FPS. It helped me keep performance in sight and avoid things that would make the game too slow on low-powered platforms.

Recent findings suggest that I feel like I threw away a lot of work during development because the art and design of the game changed several times. In hindsight, I think it was good to keep the mentality of avoiding things that would make the game slow and keeping an eye on the performance stats. But it was only towards the end of the game that I could simply focus on performance without worrying about optimizing things in a way that would make them hard to generalize or reuse in the future, since the game was finished.

It has been revealed that in the end I actually added a performance mode that tones down a few special effects, but I think it was a good decision to do that when the game was finished. Otherwise, you suddenly need to be testing and tweaking more than one version of the game while making changes and adding latest things.

Industry observers note that A frame limiter was something else I added to help slower laptops maintain a stable framerate. This also brought the necessity of adding an option to draw the cursor in hardware. For the whole development I was drawing the cursor within the game in software, and that meant some lag was unavoidable. Many customers complained about this when the demo was released.

It has been revealed that this happens when you use Vsync because the last frame you're seeing is actually buffered, so the frame is already behind the input. The OS has a special mode for drawing the cursor that prevents these issues, but then you lose the ability to apply effects to it, like fluid animations or doing some lighting around it. Being aware of this also helped me focus on reducing the input lag of the game as much as possible. When running the game with the frame limiter, you notice immediately that the cursor becomes super laggy. For that case, having a hardware cursor was necessary.

Looking back on all these details, being able to change basic engine things like that is super hard, or almost impossible, with closed engines. I worked with Unity before, doing some ports, and the mentality there was that you had to follow a set of "good practices" and deal with whatever was decided for you, even though the hardware in most cases could do better. It was very rough and slow at the beginning when making a custom engine, but the freedom you get at the end of development is very satisfying.

I feel lucky about how I got the chance to take this long journey and actually make it to the end. I feel like I stumbled into something really interesting that made me lose count of all the nice moments of realization I had while working on this project.

After all these years, I'm quite happy now to have found the perfect excuse to actually study the things I love the most to work on.

According to recent reports, if you enjoyed this article, consider giving Satelital a try. The game is available on Steam, with a free demo available.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s such a gratifying feeling that comes from finishing a really good book, closing it up, reflecting on its quality and placing it back on your bookshelf.
  • In a recent development, I spend a good deal of time flipping through autobiographies written by my favorite wrestlers, musicians and media personalities.
  • Industry observers note that chatGPT is capable of stepping up to be everyone's personal book curator.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s such a gratifying feeling that comes from finishing a really good book, closing it up, reflecting on its quality and placing it back on your bookshelf.

In a recent development, I spend a good deal of time flipping through autobiographies written by my favorite wrestlers, musicians and media personalities. Visual history books dedicated to the video games, comic books and anime I love also keep me entertained for hours. I’m always searching for the next great book that’ll keep me from staring at my phone and reading rage-baiting tweets in my spare time.

Industry observers note that chatGPT is capable of stepping up to be everyone's personal book curator. It has certainly put me on the right path to finding even more quality reads based on what it knows about the genres I like, the authors I’m a fan of and even the sort of books that I’m not really all that into.

These prompts have helped expand my collection of books, and I’m sure they’ll do the same for all my fellow bookworms reading this right now. Try any of these out and see where ChatGPT leads you next on your journey for more quality literature.

Inputting any of the following seven prompts into ChatGPT, while also providing it with your literary tastes, favorite authors, preferred styles of writing that compel you the most and current mood, will help it highlight a list of books you may end up adoring next.

The first prompt works quite well in commanding ChatGPT to examine the deeper literary qualities attached to your favorite books. The second prompt works to showcase the type of books that deliver the same type of emotional experiences you derived from your last read. The third prompt is perfect for book hunters who are on the lookout for less celebrated books that you may not have known about beforehand. The fourth prompt is the ultimate mood-book matcher, as it takes note of how you’re at the moment feeling and shows you the type of books that could get you out of a mental funk or put you in a more relaxing mood.

The fifth prompt puts ChatGPT in the mindset of a book recommendation engine that gives you the sort of books that explore genres you may have overlooked. The sixth prompt goes even further to help ChatGPT suggest what books you should read, as it mentions both your literary likes and dislikes.

As for the seventh and final prompt, it works as a survey that gives ChatGPT everything it could possibly know about you to give you the best book recommendations possible.

Feel free to refer to the seven prompts listed below and try them out for yourself to see where your next book-filled adventures lead you next:.

And as an extra follow-up response, this next prompt can help ChatGPT do another round of evaluation to see which books truly match your tastes and weed out any made-up books it may have suggested:.

Now challenge your own recommendations. Which [number] books on this list are the weakest matches for my tastes, and why? Replace them with better alternatives. Don't invent titles or authors, and tell me where you're uncertain.

Running to ChatGPT to tell it to recommend you a bunch of latest and old books worth reading without being as descriptive as possible about your tastes is a waste of time. The chatbot needs every piece of information about your interests across the literary spectrum to tailor its book recommendations to match everything you enjoy (and don’t enjoy as much).

It has been revealed that hopefully, by the end of each ChatGPT session that kicks off with any of these prompts, you’ll leave it with one or a bunch of strong suggestions that could keep you and your book club occupied for months on end. Let me know how you get on in the comments below.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

John Carpenter will return to help Zack Snyder Escape from Latest York.

In a recent development, co-written and directed by the horror icon, the 1981 sci-fi action film starred Kurt Russell as Snake Plissken, a former war hero-turned-criminal who is tasked by the government to rescue the United States President from the island of Manhattan, which has been converted into a maximum security prison in the film's dystopian future setting. Also starring Lee Van Clef, Ernest Borgnine, Isaac Hayes and Adrienne Barbeau, Escape from Latest York scored favorable reviews from critics and was a box office hit, earning both a 1996 sequel and now a remake from Snyder.

Industry observers note that during a recent appearance on Brent Spiner and Jonathan Frakes' Dropping Names podcast, Carpenter offered a brief enhancement on Snyder's Escape from Newly introduced York. The original writer/director, who is already confirmed to be an executive producer on the project, humorously revealed that he "demanded to be the composer" for the new sci-fi action remake, while also confirming that the production is "not going to use my [original] score," but that instead he and his team are "going to remake the score" from his 1981 film.

Snyder's Escape from Newly introduced York marks the latest in a string of attempts to bring the sci-fi franchise back to life going back nearly 20 years. Prior looks for the film have included everything from full-on remakes with new actors taking on the role of Snake, including Gerard Butler, while others were meant to instead be legacy sequels much in the way of 2018's Halloween. Prior to the former DC filmmaker, the movie also had everyone from Len Wiseman to Robert Rodriguez, Leigh Whannell and Radio Silence attached to direct.

Recent findings suggest that interestingly, should the film properly get off the ground, Escape from Upcoming York will also mark Snyder's first major venture back into the remake subgenre. The filmmaker memorably got his start with the James Gunn-penned remake of Dawn of the Dead, which was a critical and commercial hit and helped pave the way for his work on everything from 300 to the DC Extended Universe and his Army of the Dead franchise at Netflix.

Industry observers note that carpenter's push to be the composer for the Escape from Newly introduced York remake certainly shouldn't come as too much of a surprise. Across his 21 feature films in the director's chair, only six did not have Carpenter take on composing duties, with one of the most notable being The Thing, in which he enlisted The Good, the Bad and the Ugly's Ennio Morricone, though he still ended up adding in some of his own music.

Industry observers note that it also nicely follows in the footsteps of David Gordon Green's Halloween sequel trilogy, in which Carpenter returned as both an executive producer and composer for all three films. Moreover, the filmmaker collaborated with his son, Cody Carpenter, and Daniel Davies, with their approach being a mix of updating tracks from the original 1978 Halloween as well as bringing a new set of energetic tracks in order to tap into the different pacing of each installment.

With Carpenter confirmed for both an EP and composer role on the film, the question now becomes just how much Snyder will look to engage with his predecessor in putting together Escape from New York's script. Snyder has yet to write any of his films alone, generally partnering with Chris Terrio or Kurt Johnstad, and should he enlist input from Carpenter, it could make for a unique melding of the minds to bring a fresh take to Snake Plissken's journey.

Escape from Latest York is set in a dystopian future where Manhattan serves as a maximum-security prison. The narrative follows a former soldier sent on a perilous mission to rescue the President, who has crash-landed and been captured by the island's inmates.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it.
  • I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands.
  • According to recent reports, perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it. Here are the three main reasons why the Duo didn’t work out for me, but might for you.

I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands. You can use it one-handed, but for me it’s not nearly as comfortable as the iPhone 18 Pro. It’s too wide and too heavy to be used for long.

According to recent reports, perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions. But that would be a pretty significant shift for me, as there are so many situations when I don’t have both hands free.

If you already use two hands with your iPhone regularly—perhaps because you have a Pro Max model—then the Duo’s one-handed experience likely won’t bother you. But the more I used the Duo, the more I found myself missing my iPhone 18 Pro.

The biggest value proposition of a foldable is that it’s a 2-in-1 product, letting you have a standard phone but also a tablet-sized display that fits in your pocket.

I totally get the appeal, and fully expected to love that hybrid design. But after two weeks of trying, I still struggled to find times when I actually wanted to unfold the Duo. And to be clear, that’s a me problem, not an issue with the Duo itself.

I tried a bunch of apps on the inner display, and struggled to find use cases that—for me—made it worthwhile to open the Duo. But based on the feedback I’ve seen from most Duo owners, I’m very much in the minority.

Sources indicate that I know lots of people love the Duo for video, but I don’t watch much video on my iPhone. I almost never watch YouTube, TikTok, or Instagram Reels. And for indicates and movies, I stick with my TV screen and an Apple TV 4K.

Multitasking support on iPhone Duo works really well. But when I found myself needing to multitask, I still reached for my iPad Pro with Magic Keyboard attached. A keyboard-free product can’t replace my main computer (nor would I expect it to), and the Duo screen was too small to comfortably work on it.

Last year I bought an iPhone Air and absolutely loved it. Initially, the Air’s less capable camera system didn’t bother me, it was “good enough.”.

According to recent reports, after a few months though, I started missing the Pro camera system more. Then I learned that my wife was pregnant with twins, and I knew I wanted the best possible iPhone cameras to capture their early weeks and months. So I bought an iPhone 18 Pro in September.

Sources indicate that I’ve been very impressed by iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera upgrades, and it’s great having a Telephoto lens again too. Since having the best camera system is so crucial for me right now, I knew iPhone Duo couldn’t be my only iPhone.

I initially planned to dual-carry the two models, using iPhone 18 Pro solely as a camera. But over and over I found myself wishing it was my only iPhone.

It has been revealed that I returned mine as well. Beautiful device, but functionally not very good.

According to recent reports, is the iPhone Duo camera good enough for most people? Probably so. But for this year at least, with my twins aging rapidly, it’s not quite right for me. If I loved the Duo for other reasons, I would just use both models. But since I didn’t, I’m happy to stick with the iPhone 18 Pro.

In closing, I want to explicitly state that I don’t think the iPhone Duo is a bad product, and this isn’t a “bad review.”.

In a recent development, the iPhone Duo just isn’t for me. I get the sense, though, that it’s lots of people’s favorite iPhone in years. Apple created its most unique fresh iPhone model since the original, and there’s plenty to love about it. I’m very curious to see how popular foldables become over time compared to slab models, because each clearly offers pros and cons. But for me, at least right now, the iPhone 18 Pro is my model of choice.

Sources indicate that what has your iPhone Duo experience been like so far? Love it? Undecided? Let us know in the comments.
